Innovation and influence are very distinct phenomena. Bob Dylan, for instance, didn’t invent folk
music: He borrowed extensively from Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger and others in the folk revival
movement of the fifties and sixties, yet he became far more influential than any of them. Such is
the relationship between Warren Buffett and earlier finance and investing writers, especially
Benjamin Graham, author of The Intelligent Investor. Buffett didn’t dream up most of the ideas
that he espoused — many came straight out of Graham’s teachings — but he brought them to the
masses through the Berkshire Hathaway Inc. annual letters and gave us all a proof of concept
through the company’s extraordinary performance. In doing so, he earned his place as our greatest
investor and our leading finance and investing writer. Without Buffett, we may not be talking about
Graham at all today. So, it was with a tinge of sadness that I learned last week that Buffett was
poised to relinquish his most important annual writing exercise: the Berkshire letter. It is the end
of an era, and a time to reflect on Buffett’s accomplishments.

Over the years, Buffett’s most memorable theme was the flightiness of ‘Mr. Market’ and the need
to stay focused on intrinsic value. For Buffett, Mr. Market — a character first conceived by
Graham — was forever doomed to live with “incurable emotional problems,” as he wrote in
Berkshire’s 1987 letter4. At times Mr. Market was euphoric (prices were too high), and at others
he was deeply depressed (prices were too low), but investors always had the discretion to ignore
him or take him up on his occasionally bargain-bin prices.

The key, for Buffett, was to make sure you did your homework and had a firm grasp on the intrinsic
value of your would-be investments. “Indeed, if you aren’t certain that you understand and can
value your business far better than Mr. Market, you don’t belong in the game,” Buffett wrote. And
indeed, Buffett went on to prove that he belonged in the game, avoiding dot-com bubble stocks in
the late 1990s, building a very conservative portfolio ahead of the financial crisis, and then
pouncing when the crashes created opportunities.
SOURCE:https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2025-11-04/buffett-s-annual-letters-a-
wistful-farewell

The water was clear and bright. After days in the shade, sunlight now cut through the rough surface,
sending shimmering rays dancing across the rocky bed of the river, and illuminating the patches
of bright green algae that carpeted the rocks of deeper, slower pools. The fish gained speed, then
hurled herself above the water line, over the rocks that created a minor fall in the river. Above the
water line, the fish did not notice that the land here held only a remnant of the forest. The riverbank
was open, aside from a still-developing layer of shrubbery and the few remaining blackened
skeletal trees that dotted the riverside. The fish didn’t notice any of this, of course. She had no
awareness of the fire-scarred land or new life that was steadily reclaiming once bare soil. She
pushed ahead, moving steadily against the current. The sunlight illuminated the squirming bodies
of larvae caught in the current. The fish felt, somewhere in the recesses of her mind, the almost-
stirring of an extinguished drive-the urge to swallow them.

That urge remained a whisper in her mind. It did not surface in her body, but she felt its absence
as she swam past the would-be feast. She had once been a fish that ate larvae. Now, she was not.
Simple. She had, not so long ago, lived in the deep sea. Her lithe silver body pulled saltwater
through her gills as she explored the dark depths, feeding on its bounty. Now, she fought her way
upstream in the clear, saltless water. She remembered this taste- this fresh stream water and the
heaviness of her body in its currents. She was getting close. She did not know how she knew this
and did not wonder. But she was getting close.

She would soon make it back to the place her life had begun. There was nothing else for her. This
was right; it was where she belonged. The fish was aware that this pull was a reversal of polarity-
the same sort of tug had once compelled her down this stream and out to the sea. She had once
abandoned these shallow fresh waters for the salty depths. At the time, the need to find the sea had
felt all-consuming, and she believed she would never return to these waters. She had once raced
down these eddies with the same fervor that now compelled her to throw herself up them. She had
needed to leave. And now, she needed to return.

Sadly, the Srikakulam crowd collapse at a private, unregistered temple on a day when high footfall
was expected is hardly surprising. Reports indicate one combined entry and exit, public use of an
under-construction area, inadequate stewardship, severe capacity overshoot, and weak
infrastructure. The Hathras crowd crush in 2024 followed an event in which permission was
reportedly granted for only a third of the crowd that attended, and investigations cited inadequate
exits and gaps in planning and supervision. The 2011 Sabarimala crush also revealed systemic
weaknesses in circulation control on a day with predictable surges and a trigger that became lethal
due to constrained pathways. These incidents had different proximate triggers but the same causes
of failure: reciprocal pedestrian flows and shared gates, weak physical public infrastructure, and a
lack of real-time density monitoring. India already has guidance to anticipate these failures,
including the 2014 National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines and the National
Building Code (NBC). Indian authorities have already demonstrated a feasible path from guidance
to operations, including in recent Sabarimala seasons and with the Integrated Command and
Control Centre operating at Tirumala. This includes licensed plans compliant with NDMA or NBC
prescriptions; calculated occupancy; certified structures that prevent bidirectional flows; real-time
density control by trained stewards; and real-time communications and crowd analytics. The
persistence of stampedes stems from the gap between guidance and enforced practice.

That almost 80% of stampedes in India occur at religious gatherings or pilgrimages is not
coincidental. Pilgrim and congregational events often proceed without any licence that ties
permission to a crowd safety plan that can be tested for compliance. Authorities often infer the
capacity from the space available, rather than what can be estimated from egress options and
evacuation times, tolerate bad or no gating plans, accept temporary barricades without certified
load ratings, and do not cordon off areas with construction materials. Public safety is a process and
its absence, including during crowding disasters, is rarely due to single-point failures. The
Srikakulam incident aligns with a known risk pattern and only disciplined adoption of the
country’s own codes, enforced by licensing, will reverse it. India also needs a policy culture that
treats religious events as engineered systems requiring licensing and auditing.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/depressing-pattern-on-the-srikakulam-
stampede/article70232562.ece

Sadly, the Srikakulam crowd collapse at a private, unregistered temple on a day when high footfall
was expected is hardly surprising. Reports indicate one combined entry and exit, public use of an
under-construction area, inadequate stewardship, severe capacity overshoot, and weak
infrastructure. The Hathras crowd crush in 2024 followed an event in which permission was
reportedly granted for only a third of the crowd that attended, and investigations cited inadequate
exits and gaps in planning and supervision. The 2011 Sabarimala crush also revealed systemic
weaknesses in circulation control on a day with predictable surges and a trigger that became lethal
due to constrained pathways. These incidents had different proximate triggers but the same causes
of failure: reciprocal pedestrian flows and shared gates, weak physical public infrastructure, and a
lack of real-time density monitoring. India already has guidance to anticipate these failures,
including the 2014 National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines and the National
Building Code (NBC). Indian authorities have already demonstrated a feasible path from guidance
to operations, including in recent Sabarimala seasons and with the Integrated Command and
Control Centre operating at Tirumala. This includes licensed plans compliant with NDMA or NBC
prescriptions; calculated occupancy; certified structures that prevent bidirectional flows; real-time
density control by trained stewards; and real-time communications and crowd analytics. The
persistence of stampedes stems from the gap between guidance and enforced practice.

coincidental. Pilgrim and congregational events often proceed without any licence that ties
permission to a crowd safety plan that can be tested for compliance. Authorities often infer the
capacity from the space available, rather than what can be estimated from egress options and
evacuation times, tolerate bad or no gating plans, accept temporary barricades without certified
load ratings, and do not cordon off areas with construction materials. Public safety is a process and
its absence, including during crowding disasters, is rarely due to single-point failures. The

country’s own codes, enforced by licensing, will reverse it. India also needs a policy culture that

content.passageText:
Over the last three decades, there has been a consistent criticism of governments and private actors
who make environmental policy: Those who seek to protect “nature” know very little about living
in and with it. Arguably, aside from their good intentions, they are accused of drawing a false
disjunction between humans and the environment, including other animals. A research paper
published in Ambio surveyed 56,968 people across 61 countries to assess their level of “nature-
connectedness”. A psychological concept, nature-connectedness seeks to measure the relationship
— or lack thereof — between people and flora and fauna. Several studies have demonstrated that
such connections impact well-being and are correlated with how people act towards the
environment.

According to the study, Nepal is the most nature-connected, followed by Iran, South Africa, and
Bangladesh. India, in 22nd place, is at the upper end of the middle, while the UK, Spain, Japan,
Germany and Canada bring up the rear. Clearly, political activism is not a factor in how close
people are to nature. Germany, Canada and the UK, for example, have far stronger Green parties

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                               12 Minutes to CLAT

than Iran. But people there are, going by the study, less likely to form bonds outside of homo
sapiens. “Spirituality” correlates positively with connectedness, whereas ranking highly on the
World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business index is the opposite.

Does the study, then, insinuate at a return to the old binary between the economy and the
environment, between “development” and “growth”? Hopefully not. The better lesson to draw
from it might be to listen, learn and find a balance. The people surveyed in the countries at the top
of the list also want “development.” The answer might well be to talk to those who live with nature,
and listen to their views before planning to make cities and countries more “green” and “smart”.

The IPO (initial public offering) market in India continues to see a flurry of activity. Firms across
a range of sectors, from LG Electronics to Tata Capital, are increasingly tapping the primary
markets. And it’s not just the larger firms. In recent years, smaller and mid-sized companies, and
even start-ups, like eyewear firm Lenskart, stockbroker Groww and fintech firm Pine Labs, are
flocking to the markets. There are expectations for public offerings this year that surpass those of
last year. Globally, India, along with the US and China, accounted for the bulk of IPO activity
during the third quarter of the year as per EY. All this indicates the Indian markets' capacity to
absorb large issues.

There is a strong appetite from both institutional and retail investors; the latter are seeing
participation beyond the Tier 1 cities. The sharp increase in the number of demat accounts over
the past few years and the continuing surge in SIP flows are indicative of the growing share of

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                               12 Minutes to CLAT

household savings flowing into the markets. The stock market regulator had also recently made
changes to the IPO framework to increase institutional investor participation. But this surge in
liquidity sits uncomfortably with concerns over stretched market valuations. Questions have been
raised about the steep valuations being sought by some companies. In recent months, some IPOs
have underperformed due to aggressive pricing — shares of many companies are trading around
or below their offer price, according to some analysts. But, even IPO investors have invested for
listing-day gains — as per an earlier SEBI study, individual investors sold 50 per cent of their
shares within a week of their listing.

The public offerings can be used for various purposes — for financing firms’ expansion plans or
by existing investors, such as venture capital or private equity firms to exit. Of the Rs 1.17 lakh
crore raised this year, around a third represents investor or promoter exits as per a Kotak study.
This suggests that promoters and early investors, who hold significant stakes, are using this
opportunity to cash out, with the returns generated being either repatriated or deployed across asset
classes. Recent reports indicate that the IPO pipeline remains healthy. The sentiment among retail
investors also seems to be strong, even as the steep valuations, in some cases, are hard to ignore.

In 2026, India introduced a revised deportation policy aimed at strengthening its approach towards
illegal immigration and cross-border movement. The policy focuses on streamlining identification,
detention, and deportation procedures for foreign nationals residing in India without valid
documentation. It places particular emphasis on coordination between central agencies and state
authorities, especially in border states where issues of illegal entry and overstaying have been
prominent.

The revised framework also incorporates stricter verification mechanisms, improved data-sharing
systems, and faster processing of deportation cases. Reports indicate that the policy has been
applied in cases involving nationals from neighbouring countries, with authorities prioritising
security considerations alongside legal procedures. The development comes amid broader
concerns related to border management, demographic changes, and internal security.

The policy has also triggered discussions on humanitarian aspects, including treatment of detainees
and due process safeguards. While the government has defended the policy as necessary for
national security and administrative efficiency, critics have raised concerns about its
implementation and impact on vulnerable populations. The 2026 update marks a significant shift
in India’s approach to migration control and enforcement.

In 2026, Odisha became the first Indian state to implement a Marine Spatial Plan (MSP), marking
a significant step in coastal and marine governance. The initiative aims to regulate the use of ocean
resources by allocating specific zones for activities such as fishing, tourism, conservation, and
shipping. The plan has been developed with technical support from international organisations and
is aligned with India’s broader commitments to sustainable ocean management.

Marine Spatial Planning is a globally recognised approach used to balance ecological protection
with economic activities in marine areas. Odisha’s coastline, which stretches along the Bay of
Bengal, is ecologically sensitive and economically significant, supporting fisheries, ports, and
biodiversity hotspots. The MSP is expected to improve coordination between different
stakeholders and reduce conflicts over resource use.

The development also reflects India’s increasing focus on the blue economy, which emphasises
sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, employment, and environmental protection.
Odisha’s initiative is being seen as a pilot model that could be replicated in other coastal states in
the future.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING

The first year of the Indian Constitution's operation revealed significant judicial interpretations
that the Parliament believed hindered its socio-economic agenda. The immediate catalyst was the
Supreme Court's judgment in Romesh Thapar v. State of Madras, which struck down restrictions
on freedom of speech and expression, prompting the government to assert its legislative power.
Consequently, the Constitution First Amendment Act, 1951, was introduced to address these
judicial pronouncements and clarify constitutional intent.

The Amendment made significant alterations to fundamental rights. It amended Article 19 to
insulate laws imposing reasonable restrictions on speech. More fundamentally, it sought to protect
land reform legislation from judicial review. This was achieved by amending Article 31 to prevent
challenges to the adequacy of compensation paid for property acquired by the state. Additionally,
it introduced the Ninth Schedule, placing laws beyond judicial challenge for violating fundamental
rights.

In the realm of social justice, the Amendment inserted clauses into Articles 15 and 16 to enable
state action for backward classes. Clause four was added to Article 15, specifically empowering
the state to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward
classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. This provided
constitutional basis for affirmative action policies in educational institutions.

The constitutional validity of these changes was challenged. In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India,
the Supreme Court initially upheld the First Amendment, ruling that Parliament's power to amend

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                            12 Minutes to CLAT

 the Constitution under Article 368 extended to amending fundamental rights as well, thereby
 validating the comprehensive changes introduced by this landmark amendment.

content.passageText:
The evolution of international air law from the Paris Convention of 1919 to the Chicago
 Convention of 1944 represents a fundamental shift in the regulation of global aviation,
 transitioning from a primarily European-centric framework to a truly international system designed

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                                12 Minutes to CLAT

 to accommodate the explosive growth of air travel following World War II. The Paris Convention,
 officially the Convention Relating to the Regulation of Aerial Navigation, was the first
 comprehensive international agreement to codify the principle of state sovereignty over airspace,
 declaring that every state had complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its
 territory.

 This foundational concept, enshrined in its Article 1, directly countered earlier proposals that
 airspace should be considered free and open, much like the high seas. The Paris Convention
 established the International Commission for Air Navigation, which was tasked with collecting
 data and proposing amendments to technical annexes concerning matters like aircraft registration,
 airworthiness, and navigation maps. However, the Paris framework was limited in its global reach,
 as it was largely a product of European powers and did not secure universal participation.
 Moreover, it drew a clear distinction between civil aircraft and state aircraft, such as military and
 customs aircraft, with the latter category being excluded from the right of innocent passage and
 requiring special authorization to overfly or land in foreign territories.

 This principle of nationality, wherein an aircraft possessed the legal character of the state in which
 it was registered, was firmly established and required that registration be made in a public register
 accessible to other states. The onset of World War II, however, demonstrated both the inadequacies
 of the Paris regime and the immense strategic importance of air power, prompting Allied nations
 to begin planning for a new post-war order even as hostilities continued. This planning culminated
 in the Chicago Convention of 1944, which fundamentally restructured international air law by
 creating the International Civil Aviation Organization as a permanent specialized agency of the
 United Nations to oversee cooperation and standard setting.

 The Chicago Convention reaffirmed the core principle of absolute sovereignty from Paris, but
 expanded its scope by explicitly addressing both scheduled and non-scheduled air services,
 establishing the five freedoms of the air through separate agreements, and mandating that all
 charges for airports and air navigation facilities be published and communicated to ICAO. It also
 refined the classification of aircraft, ensuring that the nationality principle applied uniformly to all
 aircraft engaged in international navigation, while continuing to exempt state aircraft from
 automatic overflight rights. The Chicago regime thus created a durable legal architecture balancing
 national sovereignty with the practical necessities of international air commerce.

Every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory.
Airspace shall be divided into international zones managed by ICAO.

National sovereignty extends indefinitely into outer space.

content.passageText:
The functional phase of a treaty, following its entry into force, is governed by established rules
 regarding its observance, application, and interpretation. These principles, primarily codified in
 the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), ensure stability in international relations.
 The cornerstone is pacta sunt servanda (Article 26), which mandates that every treaty in force is
 binding upon the parties and must be performed by them in good faith. Reinforcing this, Article

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                                12 Minutes to CLAT

 27 prevents a state from invoking its internal law, including its constitution, as a justification for
 treaty non-compliance.

 The application of treaties is subject to specific parameters. Under Article 28, treaties are not
 retroactive, meaning they do not bind a party regarding acts or facts that occurred before the treaty's
 entry into force for that state. Article 29 establishes that a treaty binds each party in respect of its
 entire territory, unless a contrary intention is expressed. Where states conclude successive treaties
 on the same subject, Article 30 provides the framework for determining which instrument prevails.

 The interpretation of treaties is governed by a general rule articulated in Articles 31-33. The
 primary approach is textual: a treaty must be interpreted in good faith according to the ordinary
 meaning of its terms in their context, and in light of its object and purpose. The context includes
 the preamble and annexes. Crucially, subsequent agreements between the parties on interpretation,
 and their subsequent practice in applying the treaty, are to be taken into account. Supplementary
 means, such as the negotiating history (travaux préparatoires), may only be consulted to confirm
 the meaning derived from this general rule, or when the primary interpretation leaves the meaning
 ambiguous.

 Separate from questions of application are grounds that can invalidate a treaty, rendering it void
 ab initio. A treaty is void if it conflicts with a peremptory norm of general international law (jus
 cogens), such as a treaty authorizing genocide (Article 53). Consent to be bound may also be
 invalidated by error (Article 48), fraud (Article 49), corruption of a state representative (Article
 50), or coercion of a representative or of a state by the threat or use of force (Articles 51 and 52).
 Furthermore, a state may invoke that its consent was invalid due to a manifest violation of a
 fundamental rule of its internal law regarding treaty competence (Article 46).
content.questionText:

    perpetual docking rights at State A's Port Harbor. In 2024, a new government in State A cited
    national security concerns and issued a decree suspending all docking privileges for State B,
    arguing its sovereignty allows it to prioritize security over treaty commitments. Under
    international law, what is the correct outcome?
options:
State A must continue performing the treaty in good faith as it remains binding despite
           the change in government policy.

State A can terminate the treaty unilaterally because the decree represents a valid exercise
           of sovereign legislative power and cannot be questioned by another state.

State A must renegotiate the treaty terms with State B while it conducts a formal review
           of the treaty's security implications.

State A may suspend the treaty unilaterally and indefinitely because national security
           concerns automatically override any prior treaty obligations undertaken by a sovereign
           state.

content.passageText:
The cornerstone of statutory administrative law in India is the concept of delegated legislation,
wherein the legislature delegates its law-making power to the executive. The fountainhead of this
authority is the Parent Act, also known as the enabling Act. For instance, The Air (Prevention and
Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, serves as a classic illustration; while it establishes the broad
framework for pollution control, it specifically empowers the Central Government to formulate
detailed rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. This delegation is a practical necessity,
allowing the executive to address technical and situational details that the legislature cannot
feasibly handle.

The output of this delegated power manifests in various forms, including Rules, Regulations, By-
laws, Orders, and Notifications. While these instruments have the force of law, they are created by
administrative bodies, not Parliament. To ensure this vast power is not misused, the Indian legal
framework provides robust mechanisms of control. Paramount among these is Parliamentary
control, exercised through specialized bodies like the Committee on Subordinate Legislation in
both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. These committees scrutinize delegated legislation to ensure
it does not exceed the authority granted by the parent Act or trespass upon citizens' rights. A key
procedural tool is the inclusion of "laying" clauses in the Parent Act, which requires that the rules
made be placed before Parliament. This allows for legislative oversight, where such rules can be
modified or annulled.

Beyond parliamentary oversight, strict procedural requirements govern the lifecycle of these rules.
The General Clauses Act, 1897, particularly Sections 20 to 22, provides the statutory backbone for
these procedures. These sections deal with the crucial aspects of when a rule is considered to have
been made and the power to bring it into force. Finally, the principle of publication is fundamental.
For any rule, regulation, or notification to acquire the binding force of law, it must be published in
the Official Gazette. This mandatory publication serves as formal notice to the public, transforming
a draft into an enforceable legal instrument and upholding the rule of law by ensuring transparency
and accessibility.

content.questionText:
The Palampur Municipal Corporation issued a notification mandating solar panels on all
    residential buildings, claiming inherent power to govern civic amenities. However, its Parent
    Act only grants authority over "water supply and drainage" with no mention of renewable
    energy. Is this notification legally valid?
options:
The notification is valid because the executive can fill gaps in legislation whenever it
           deems necessary for public welfare without express authorization.

The notification is invalid because all forms of delegated legislation require prior
           approval from the President of India before being enforced.

The notification is valid because municipalities have residual powers to govern local
           amenities not specifically mentioned in their enabling Act.

The notification is invalid because delegated legislation must derive its authority from a
           specific power granted within the Parent Act, and no such power exists here.

content.passageText:
The cornerstone of statutory administrative law in India is the concept of delegated legislation,
wherein the legislature delegates its law-making power to the executive. The fountainhead of this
authority is the Parent Act, also known as the enabling Act. For instance, The Air (Prevention and
Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, serves as a classic illustration; while it establishes the broad
framework for pollution control, it specifically empowers the Central Government to formulate
detailed rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act. This delegation is a practical necessity,
allowing the executive to address technical and situational details that the legislature cannot
feasibly handle.

The output of this delegated power manifests in various forms, including Rules, Regulations, By-
laws, Orders, and Notifications. While these instruments have the force of law, they are created by
administrative bodies, not Parliament. To ensure this vast power is not misused, the Indian legal
framework provides robust mechanisms of control. Paramount among these is Parliamentary
control, exercised through specialized bodies like the Committee on Subordinate Legislation in
both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. These committees scrutinize delegated legislation to ensure
it does not exceed the authority granted by the parent Act or trespass upon citizens' rights. A key
procedural tool is the inclusion of "laying" clauses in the Parent Act, which requires that the rules
made be placed before Parliament. This allows for legislative oversight, where such rules can be
modified or annulled.

Beyond parliamentary oversight, strict procedural requirements govern the lifecycle of these rules.
The General Clauses Act, 1897, particularly Sections 20 to 22, provides the statutory backbone for
these procedures. These sections deal with the crucial aspects of when a rule is considered to have
been made and the power to bring it into force. Finally, the principle of publication is fundamental.
For any rule, regulation, or notification to acquire the binding force of law, it must be published in
the Official Gazette. This mandatory publication serves as formal notice to the public, transforming
a draft into an enforceable legal instrument and upholding the rule of law by ensuring transparency
and accessibility.

content.passageText:
The Stockholm Declaration, formally known as the Declaration of the United Nations Conference
 on the Human Environment, was adopted in 1972 and is widely regarded as the foundational
 instrument of modern international environmental law. Emerging from the first major global
 conference to make the environment a principal subject of international concern, the Declaration
 consisted of a preamble and twenty-six principles intended to guide the preservation and
 enhancement of the human environment. Its historical significance lies in its articulation of core
 legal concepts that would later crystallize into binding treaty obligations and customary
 international law.

 Principle 21, perhaps the most influential provision, proclaimed that states have the sovereign right
 to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental policies, but also the
 responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not cause damage to
 the environment of other states or of areas beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. This carefully
 balanced formulation reconciled the competing claims of territorial sovereignty and transboundary
 environmental protection, embedding the essence of the no-harm rule into the international legal
 consciousness. The Declaration also introduced the concept that environmental protection is not
 merely a national concern but a shared responsibility of humanity, with Principle 1 declaring that
 man bears a solemn responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future
 generations, thereby planting the seeds of the principle of intergenerational equity.

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                              12 Minutes to CLAT


 Furthermore, it called for international cooperation to address environmental challenges,
 encouraged the exchange of scientific information, and urged states to develop national
 environmental laws and institutions. While the Stockholm Declaration itself was not a legally
 binding treaty, its principles have been extensively cited in subsequent international agreements,
 judicial decisions, and state practice, effectively shaping the normative framework within which
 contemporary environmental governance operates. It paved the way for later developments such
 as the Rio Declaration, the establishment of the United Nations Environment Programme, and the
 negotiation of countless multilateral environmental agreements addressing issues ranging from
 ozone depletion to biodiversity loss. The Declaration remains a touchstone for environmental
 diplomacy, embodying the international community’s early recognition that economic
 development must be reconciled with ecological sustainability.

content.passageText:
The Specific Relief Act, 1963, provides the juridical foundation for enforcing individual civil
 rights when monetary compensation is inadequate. A primary remedy under this legislation is the
 Recovering of Possession of Property, which focuses on restoring physical control over a thing
 rather than its pecuniary value. Regarding immovable property, such as land or buildings, the Act
 provides recourse for two categories of plaintiffs. First, a person who has been wrongly
 dispossessed can file a suit for possession based on their legal title, seeking to reclaim what is
 rightfully theirs. Second, and critically, the Act protects a person who may not have perfect title
 but was in prior possession. Rooted in the principle that no one should take the law into their own
 hands, it mandates that even a person with prior possession cannot be forcibly evicted; the rightful
 owner must seek recourse through due process of law. For movable property, the remedy allows a
 person entitled to immediate possession of a specific, identifiable chattel—such as a family
 heirloom, a unique piece of art, or a specific antique—to sue for the return of that exact object,
 recognizing its special value that cannot be replicated by a damages claim.

 Equally central to the Act is the remedy of Specific Performance of Contracts, which compels a
 defaulting party to actually perform the positive obligations they undertook in an agreement, rather
 than simply paying compensation for its breach. The jurisdiction of the court to grant this relief is
 guided by the Act's provisions. Specific performance is typically decreed for contracts where
 damages would be an inadequate remedy. These include contracts for the transfer of immovable
 property, like a sale of a house, where every piece of land is considered unique. It also applies to
 contracts for the transfer of movable property that has special or unique value, such as rare shares
 or heirlooms, as well as contracts involving a fiduciary relationship, where the element of personal
 trust is paramount. Conversely, the Act explicitly bars the enforcement of certain categories of
 contracts. The court will not order specific performance of contracts that require constant
 supervision, such as detailed building contracts. It also refuses to enforce contracts for personal
 service, grounded in the principle that forcing a singer to perform would amount to involuntary
 servitude. Furthermore, contracts that are vague, uncertain in their terms, or which have become
 impossible to perform will not be specifically enforced, ensuring that the court's equitable power
 is exercised only where a clear, binding obligation exists.

The court will direct Priya to pay monetary compensation to Rohan for his loss of shelter

 rather than its pecuniary value. Regarding immovable property, such as land or buildings, the Act
 provides recourse for two categories of plaintiffs. First, a person who has been wrongly
 dispossessed can file a suit for possession based on their legal title, seeking to reclaim what is
 rightfully theirs. Second, and critically, the Act protects a person who may not have perfect title
 but was in prior possession. Rooted in the principle that no one should take the law into their own
 hands, it mandates that even a person with prior possession cannot be forcibly evicted; the rightful
 owner must seek recourse through due process of law. For movable property, the remedy allows a
 person entitled to immediate possession of a specific, identifiable chattel—such as a family
 heirloom, a unique piece of art, or a specific antique—to sue for the return of that exact object,
 recognizing its special value that cannot be replicated by a damages claim.

 Equally central to the Act is the remedy of Specific Performance of Contracts, which compels a
 defaulting party to actually perform the positive obligations they undertook in an agreement, rather
 than simply paying compensation for its breach. The jurisdiction of the court to grant this relief is
 guided by the Act's provisions. Specific performance is typically decreed for contracts where
 damages would be an inadequate remedy. These include contracts for the transfer of immovable
 property, like a sale of a house, where every piece of land is considered unique. It also applies to
 contracts for the transfer of movable property that has special or unique value, such as rare shares
 or heirlooms, as well as contracts involving a fiduciary relationship, where the element of personal
 trust is paramount. Conversely, the Act explicitly bars the enforcement of certain categories of
 contracts. The court will not order specific performance of contracts that require constant
 supervision, such as detailed building contracts. It also refuses to enforce contracts for personal
 service, grounded in the principle that forcing a singer to perform would amount to involuntary
 servitude. Furthermore, contracts that are vague, uncertain in their terms, or which have become
 impossible to perform will not be specifically enforced, ensuring that the court's equitable power
 is exercised only where a clear, binding obligation exists.

content.passageText:
When wealthy nations import steel, cement, or aluminium from countries with weaker climate
 regulations, they gain a competitive advantage that has nothing to do with genuine efficiency. The
 producing country has simply offloaded the environmental cost onto the planet. This phenomenon,
 called carbon leakage, undermines the entire logic of domestic carbon pricing: if a nation taxes its
 own industries for emitting greenhouse gases but allows untaxed foreign competitors to fill the
 gap, total global emissions may not fall at all. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism,
 introduced by the European Union and set to apply fully from 2026, attempts to correct this
 distortion. Under the scheme, importers of certain carbon-intensive goods must purchase
 certificates matching the carbon price that would have been paid had the goods been produced
 under EU rules. Proponents argue that this levels the playing field and gives exporting nations an
 incentive to adopt their own carbon pricing regimes. Critics raise three objections. First, the
 mechanism functions as a form of trade protectionism dressed in environmental language, since it
 disproportionately burdens developing economies whose industries are both more carbon-
 intensive and less able to absorb higher costs. Second, the scheme covers only a narrow range of
 goods; most emissions-intensive products, such as electronics and textiles, fall outside its scope,
 limiting its overall impact. Third, assessing the embedded carbon in imported goods requires
 accurate data that many exporting nations lack the administrative capacity to provide, raising the
 risk of arbitrary and contestable calculations. Defenders respond that imperfect border measures
 are better than no measures, and that the revenue generated could fund climate finance for
 developing nations. The deeper question is whether climate policy and trade policy can be
 reconciled without wealthy nations using environmental goals as cover for economic self-interest.

content.passageText:
Most people are aware that they procrastinate, yet awareness alone rarely cures the habit. The
 standard explanation is laziness, but psychologists have largely abandoned this account.
 Procrastination is better understood as a failure of self-regulation driven by present bias: the human

CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 18                                              12 Minutes to CLAT

 tendency to assign disproportionate weight to immediate discomfort relative to future benefit.
 When a task is unpleasant, boring, or anxiety-inducing, the emotional cost of starting it feels
 concrete and immediate, while the reward of completing it feels abstract and distant. The rational
 calculus points clearly toward starting, but the emotional calculus overrides it. This framing
 matters because it shifts the target of intervention. If procrastination were simply laziness, the
 remedy would be willpower or moral exhortation. But if it is a predictable feature of how human
 minds discount the future, more structural solutions become relevant. Breaking a task into smaller
 sub-tasks reduces the emotional cost of beginning, since each sub-task feels less overwhelming
 than the whole. Implementation intentions -- specific plans linking a situation to an action ("When
 I sit down after dinner, I will write for twenty minutes") -- exploit the brain's tendency to automate
 routine-associated behaviour, reducing the moment-to-moment decision load. Critics of the
 present-bias account argue that some procrastination is rational. Waiting for more information
 before beginning a task, or allowing unconscious processing to generate better solutions, can lead
 to higher-quality outcomes. The surgeon who delays a non-emergency procedure while reviewing
 new evidence is not behaving irrationally. Distinguishing productive delay from self-defeating
 avoidance requires attention to whether the delay is goal-directed or whether it is accompanied by
 guilt, rising anxiety, and last-minute rushes that erode the quality of the final output. The evidence
 suggests that the most effective interventions target the emotional barrier rather than the cognitive
 one. Self-compassion -- treating oneself with understanding after procrastinating rather than with
 harsh self-criticism -- consistently reduces future procrastination, possibly because guilt itself
 triggers avoidance of the task that caused it. [Extracted with revisions and edits from research
 summaries in Psychological Bulletin and the American Psychological Association.]

 standard explanation is laziness, but psychologists have largely abandoned this account.
 Procrastination is better understood as a failure of self-regulation driven by present bias: the human

 matters because it shifts the target of intervention. If procrastination were simply laziness, the

 routine-associated behaviour, reducing the moment-to-moment decision load. Critics of the
 present-bias account argue that some procrastination is rational. Waiting for more information
 before beginning a task, or allowing unconscious processing to generate better solutions, can lead

 avoidance requires attention to whether the delay is goal-directed or whether it is accompanied by
 guilt, rising anxiety, and last-minute rushes that erode the quality of the final output. The evidence

impacted his overall earnings.

ENGLISH LANGUAGE


The Supreme Court recently pulled up the Maharashtra government for its poor performance in
implementing afforestation measures as compensation for cutting down trees while constructing
Mumbai Metro lines. Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation's measures, including tree transplantation,
were undertaken so ineffectively that it was obvious that compensatory and mitigation measures
are not high on the priority list while building critical infrastructure.


Developers are required to undertake compensatory afforestation when their projects involve
diversion of forest land or felling of trees. They are also required to implement measures to
mitigate the environmental impacts of their development. But there is a tendency to take a box-
ticking approach to such obligations. With climate and ecological risks rising, it is essential that
economic activities - like infra development projects - begin to take measures that hedge against
these risks. Understanding risks and the role that compensatory afforestation and environmental
mitigation play in reducing them will push developers to treat them as integral parts of project
design, rather than afterthoughts.


The top court pulling up Maharashtra government should serve as a wake-up call for
policymakers to systemically incorporate ecological and climate factors in their planning. Even
when infrastructure is considered green - as in the case of metro lines or RE transmission
networks - environmental impacts remain. Ensuring that these impacts are addressed is critical
for building resilient infrastructure. The apex court's rap on the state government's knuckles
should nudge both public and private developers, as well as policymakers, to review how they
understand and address climate and ecological risks.

green-test/articleshow/125037926.cms

ENGLISH LANGUAGE


The Supreme Court recently pulled up the Maharashtra government for its poor performance in
implementing afforestation measures as compensation for cutting down trees while constructing
Mumbai Metro lines. Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation's measures, including tree transplantation,
were undertaken so ineffectively that it was obvious that compensatory and mitigation measures
are not high on the priority list while building critical infrastructure.


Developers are required to undertake compensatory afforestation when their projects involve
diversion of forest land or felling of trees. They are also required to implement measures to
mitigate the environmental impacts of their development. But there is a tendency to take a box-
ticking approach to such obligations. With climate and ecological risks rising, it is essential that
economic activities - like infra development projects - begin to take measures that hedge against
these risks. Understanding risks and the role that compensatory afforestation and environmental
mitigation play in reducing them will push developers to treat them as integral parts of project
design, rather than afterthoughts.


The top court pulling up Maharashtra government should serve as a wake-up call for
policymakers to systemically incorporate ecological and climate factors in their planning. Even
when infrastructure is considered green - as in the case of metro lines or RE transmission
networks - environmental impacts remain. Ensuring that these impacts are addressed is critical
for building resilient infrastructure. The apex court's rap on the state government's knuckles
should nudge both public and private developers, as well as policymakers, to review how they
understand and address climate and ecological risks.

This is something ’90s kids from smaller cities would remember: Lying on the terrace during
power cuts, staring at the night sky, counting stars, tracing constellations, and marvelling at that
hazy band of white light, the Milky Way. That view has vanished from Indian cities, even after a
cleansing evening rain. The culprit: Light pollution. As cities battle filthy rivers and toxic air,
with cloud seeding now the latest half-measure, few mention another pollutant — the constant
glow that is erasing the stars. We have flooded our nights with brightness so thoroughly that we
have forgotten what darkness feels like. There is something tragic about how our love of light
has become overexposure. What began as a victory over fear and darkness has turned into a
kind of planetary insomnia. The skies above cities never truly darken; they linger in a tired


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                    4


amber haze. Street- lights, billboards and glass towers spill photons skywards, bleaching the
heavens that once kept our time. Worse, we have learned to celebrate it. Satellite images of
glittering cities are passed around on social media as postcards of progress. India’s nighttime
glow has become a staple in growth story decks, every halo read as proof of prosperity. But
those glowing rings mark not success but waste, light meant for the streets lost to the sky.


The fallout runs deeper than aesthetics. Human biology ticks to the rhythm of light and dark, the
circadian cycle that keeps our sleep, hormones and metabolism in tune. Artificial light at night
knocks that balance off-kilter. A study in West Bengal found that city dwellers surrounded by
night-time radiance reported poorer sleep. Another, in Sleep and Vigilance, showed how light
pollution suppresses melatonin, the hormone that repairs cells and regulates rest. For other
species too, darkness is survival. Bats abandon feeding routes under harsh LED glare. Insects
spin around bulbs until they die of exhaustion. Each night, our lights erase a little more of the
planet’s nocturnal life. India has always revered light, though not this kind.


Progress should not be judged by how brightly our cities glow from space, but by how clearly we
can see the stars from our rooftops. Perhaps the first act of real advancement is as simple as
switching off an unnecessary light and looking up long enough to remember what we have lost.
If we can once again lie under a real night sky, trace Orion and find that faint, milky ribbon
above, we might rediscover not just the stars but something quietly illuminated within ourselves.

Mad mathematics – that’s what nuke competition is. Nuclear-armed countries have enough
warheads to destroy the world many times over. But most want more. And it’s no surprise that
Trump has ordered the resumption of nuclear testing. He claims Russia, China and North Korea
are doing it. There’s no proof Moscow and Beijing are mushroom-clouding again. Yes, Kim
Jong Un is. But he runs a rogue regime. Trump’s real motivation is mad math. Putin is expanding
his nuclear weapons delivery systems. Xi wants 1,000 nukes by 2030. But Trump has multiple
delivery options too, and he can feel damn macho by asking generals to tell him about America’s
5,000 nukes. So, what’s bugging him? Answer: Nuke geopolitics is crazy.


Israel has nukes but doesn’t deny or confirm it. America lets it be. But Israel’s adversaries think
of going nuclear. Other nuke-seeking nations argue that nukes will make them safer – they point
to Libya, which gave up nuke ambitions and is in chaos, to Ukraine, which gave up nukes and
got invaded by Putin. Even a child knows a nuclear war has no winner. But apparently, govts
have a hard time understanding this.


The nuclear arms race however, has one clear winner – the arms lobby. Backward linkages of
nuclear testing directly benefit arms manufacturers. They are in clover anyway, given the
number of conflicts going on in the world. Look closely, there’s a pattern. Sow chaos, supply
weapons to conflicting sides, which in turn creates more chaos and finally forces warring parties
to consider nukes. Globally, the military-industrial complex is getting fat on a market worth
approximately $2.5tn annually. But it wants more. The likes of Trump, who, btw, wants the


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                   7


Nobel Peace Prize, are happy to feed that greed. And the math gets madder.

The discharge of AAP leader Arvind Kejriwal in the Delhi excise policy case is not merely a
personal reprieve for a former chief minister. It is a pointed reminder that the criminal justice
system cannot be reduced to a political instrument without cost to its own credibility. Mr
Kejriwal’s arrest in March 2024, weeks before the general election, was always going to be read
through a political lens. As the leader of the Aam Aadmi Party and the sitting chief minister of
Delhi at the time, he was no minor figure. The Central Bureau of Investigation alleged that the
government’s 2021 liquor policy was crafted to benefit select private players. The policy was


12minutestoclat.com                                                                            9


scrapped amid controversy, and a corruption case followed, ensnaring senior leaders such as
Manish Sisodia and Sanjay Singh. Yet after nearly two years of investigation, arrest, denial of bail,
and courtroom drama, the trial court concluded there was no overarching conspiracy and no
demonstrable criminal intent. Even more striking was its criticism of the CBI’s methods – faulting
it for building a narrative on conjecture and on statements of approvers rather than on evidence.


This is the part that should trouble anyone concerned with institutional integrity. The CBI occupies
a unique place in India’s governance architecture. It reports to the Union government but is
expected to function as an independent investigative arm. Its credibility depends not only on
securing convictions but on demonstrating procedural fairness. When courts begin to question the
foundation of its investigations, the damage extends beyond a single case. The political context
cannot be wished away. The Bharatiya Janata Party, which governs at the Centre, has repeatedly
denied using investigative agencies to target opposition leaders.


However, a pattern of high-profile arrests of opposition figures — often timed around elections –
has fuelled scepticism. The Kejriwal case will inevitably reinforce that perception, whether or not
it reflects intent. None of this implies that elected officials should be shielded from scrutiny. On
the contrary, robust investigation of corruption is essential in a democracy. But robustness is not
the same as aggression. The rule of law requires evidence that can withstand judicial scrutiny, not
headlines that can dominate a news cycle.. The real defendant in this episode was not a former
chief minister. It was the credibility of India’s investigative institutions. And that trial, unlike the
excise policy, is far from over.

content.passageText:
It may seem absurd to many that a festival of ghosts, witches and monsters should be celebrated
with such enthusiasm each year in a country where daily life has enough actual horror. This
certainly is one big justification offered by those who mock people for wearing plastic fangs and
capes and taking their kids trick-or-treating on October 31. Then there are the usual sanskaar-based
arguments trotted out by uncles and aunties on all occasions from Valentine’s Day to
Thanksgiving, and the shaming by those who see in these celebrations yet another occasion for the
sitcom-conditioned minds of urban Indians to spend their hard-earned money on tawdry decor and
tacky costumes.


From another perspective, however, Halloween need not be seen as a mere import or even just an
occasion to party in strange costumes and drink too much. It could, indeed, be recast as a mirror
for the scary realities of the everyday. After all, the spooky elements for scary season are all right
there and on view all through the year — from the ghosts of unfinished infrastructure projects and
forgotten poll promises to the hair-raising revisions to school and college fees. One can see them
in the fright-inducing electricity bills, the gaping potholes that threaten to swallow one’s vehicle
whole and the annual medical reports of those living through the high-AQI hell.


Some hoary Halloween traditions, in fact, could well be imparting skills essential for surviving
many of these mundane horrors. Listening to ghost stories, for example, could numb one to the
terror that words can induce — crucial, for example, when the boss requests “a quick Monday


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                12


morning meeting”, or when the landlord texts about raising the rent and the bank sends a reminder
about an upcoming EMI payment. A little trick-or-treating harms no one and could well make the
24/7 terror of modern life a little more bearable.

modern-life-bearable-10338860/

The Greater Nicobar Project has emerged as one of India’s most ambitious infrastructure
initiatives, aimed at transforming Great Nicobar Island into a major economic and strategic hub.
The project includes the development of a transshipment port, an international airport, power
infrastructure, and urban settlements. Its location near key international shipping routes adds to its
strategic importance for trade and maritime security.

The island lies close to the __________, one of the busiest maritime chokepoints in the world,
through which a significant portion of global trade passes. This makes the project crucial for
enhancing India’s presence in the Indo-Pacific region. However, the initiative has also generated
environmental concerns, as the island is home to rich biodiversity, dense forests, and indigenous
tribal communities.

Debates surrounding the project have focused on balancing economic development with ecological
conservation and protection of indigenous rights. Environmental assessments, forest clearances,
and long-term sustainability remain central to discussions on the project’s implementation. The
Greater Nicobar Project reflects the intersection of development, environmental policy, and
strategic geopolitics in India.

LEGAL REASONING


The evolution of international environmental law represents a fascinating journey from bilateral
treaties addressing narrow concerns to a complex web of multilateral agreements governing the
global commons. Prior to the twentieth century, environmental issues were primarily addressed
through property law or bilateral disputes concerning shared resources such as rivers or fisheries.
The industrial revolution, however, unleashed unprecedented environmental degradation that
transcended national boundaries, necessitating a coordinated international response.


The true genesis of modern international environmental law is often traced to the early 1970s,
when the international community began to recognize that environmental protection was not
merely a matter of domestic policy but a collective responsibility of all nations. This recognition
culminated in a landmark conference that produced a declaration containing twenty-six principles
aimed at inspiring and guiding the peoples of the world in the preservation and enhancement of
the human environment. The declaration articulated fundamental rights and responsibilities,
including the principle that states have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant
to their environmental policies, coupled with the responsibility to ensure that activities within their
jurisdiction do not cause damage to the environment of other states.


Two decades later, another historic conference was convened to address the accelerating
environmental challenges facing the planet, resulting in a comprehensive program of action for
sustainable development in the twenty-first century. This conference produced a declaration that


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 23


 built upon its predecessor while introducing new principles tailored to contemporary challenges.
 Among these was the formal articulation of principles that have since become cornerstones of
 international environmental jurisprudence, including the concept that where there are threats of
 serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for
 postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. The conference also
 produced a non-binding statement of principles for the sustainable management of forests and
 facilitated the opening for signature of two significant conventions addressing climate change and
 biological diversity.

content.passageText:
The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provides a framework for the invalidity,
 termination, and suspension of treaties, balancing the principle of pacta sunt servanda with the
 need for flexibility in exceptional circumstances. One ground for termination is supervening
 impossibility of performance under Article 61. This occurs when an object indispensable for the
 treaty's execution permanently disappears, such as the submergence of an island that was the sole
 subject of a territorial agreement.


 A much narrower ground is the fundamental change of circumstances, or rebus sic stantibus, found
 in Article 62. This is not a simple escape clause. It applies only when an unforeseen change
 radically transforms the extent of obligations still to be performed. The circumstances must have
 constituted an essential basis of consent, and the change must not result from a breach by the party


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                                   25


 invoking it. Boundary treaties are explicitly excluded from this rule, making it exceptionally
 difficult to prove.


 External events like the severance of diplomatic relations are addressed in Article 63. Such
 severance does not automatically terminate or suspend treaties between the parties, unless the
 existence of diplomatic relations is indispensable for the treaty's application. A more profound
 basis for termination arises under Article 64 concerning the emergence of a new jus cogens norm.
 If a new peremptory norm of general international law emerges, any existing treaty in conflict with
 it becomes void and terminates, ensuring the legal order can invalidate agreements that become
 fundamentally incompatible with its core values.


 The consequences of these events are outlined in Articles 69 and 70. For void treaties, such as
 those conflicting with jus cogens, acts performed in good faith before the invalidity are not
 rendered unlawful. For terminated treaties, parties are released from future obligations. However,
 any rights or legal situations created through the treaty's execution prior to its termination are
 preserved, maintaining legal stability. This framework ensures that while treaties are binding, their
 dissolution is possible in a controlled and orderly manner when confronted with truly fundamental
 changes.

content.passageText:
The constitutional conflict between Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and the
 protection of fundamental rights reached a critical juncture in the landmark case of I.C. Golak Nath
 v. State of Punjab in 1967. The central question before the Supreme Court was whether Parliament
 could amend fundamental rights under Article 368, or whether such rights were immutable and
 beyond the reach of the amending process. The petitioners argued that fundamental rights,
 enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, were given a transcendental position and were not subject
 to abridgment or repeal by the amending procedure. They contended that an amendment under
 Article 368 was essentially a legislative process and would therefore be considered a law under
 Article 13, which prohibits the state from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental
 rights.


 The majority judgment, delivered by Chief Justice Subba Rao, held that an amendment under
 Article 368 was indeed a law within the meaning of Article 13. Consequently, if a constitutional
 amendment sought to abridge or take away any fundamental right, it would be declared void. This
 decision sent shockwaves through the political establishment, as it effectively placed fundamental
 rights outside the scope of the amendment process and threatened to invalidate previous
 amendments that had restricted property rights and other provisions. The judgment also introduced
 the doctrine of prospective overruling to ensure that its effects would not unsettle past
 amendments, but it nonetheless created a constitutional impasse.


 Parliament viewed this restriction as an impediment to its ability to implement socio-economic
 reforms through constitutional changes. The political climate demanded a response that would
 restore Parliament's authority to amend any part of the Constitution, including fundamental rights,
 while also clarifying the nature of the amending power. This constitutional deadlock set the stage
 for a direct confrontation between the legislative and judicial branches, ultimately leading to a
 significant constitutional amendment designed to explicitly overturn the effects of the Golak Nath
 ruling and reassert Parliament's supremacy in the amendment process.

content.passageText:
The constitutional conflict between Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and the
 protection of fundamental rights reached a critical juncture in the landmark case of I.C. Golak Nath
 v. State of Punjab in 1967. The central question before the Supreme Court was whether Parliament
 could amend fundamental rights under Article 368, or whether such rights were immutable and
 beyond the reach of the amending process. The petitioners argued that fundamental rights,
 enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, were given a transcendental position and were not subject
 to abridgment or repeal by the amending procedure. They contended that an amendment under
 Article 368 was essentially a legislative process and would therefore be considered a law under
 Article 13, which prohibits the state from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental
 rights.


 The majority judgment, delivered by Chief Justice Subba Rao, held that an amendment under
 Article 368 was indeed a law within the meaning of Article 13. Consequently, if a constitutional
 amendment sought to abridge or take away any fundamental right, it would be declared void. This
 decision sent shockwaves through the political establishment, as it effectively placed fundamental
 rights outside the scope of the amendment process and threatened to invalidate previous
 amendments that had restricted property rights and other provisions. The judgment also introduced
 the doctrine of prospective overruling to ensure that its effects would not unsettle past
 amendments, but it nonetheless created a constitutional impasse.


 Parliament viewed this restriction as an impediment to its ability to implement socio-economic
 reforms through constitutional changes. The political climate demanded a response that would
 restore Parliament's authority to amend any part of the Constitution, including fundamental rights,
 while also clarifying the nature of the amending power. This constitutional deadlock set the stage
 for a direct confrontation between the legislative and judicial branches, ultimately leading to a
 significant constitutional amendment designed to explicitly overturn the effects of the Golak Nath
 ruling and reassert Parliament's supremacy in the amendment process.

content.passageText:
The transfer of ownership, or "property," in goods is a pivotal concept under the Sale of Goods
Act, 1930, as it dictates when the risk and title pass from seller to buyer. The Act provides a clear
framework in Sections 18 through 24, distinguishing between specific goods, unascertained goods,
and goods delivered on approval.


For specific or ascertained goods, which are identified at the time of the contract, the transfer of
ownership depends on the state of the goods and the completion of any necessary formalities.
Section 20 states that in an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property
passes to the buyer immediately upon contract formation. Crucially, this occurs irrespective of
whether payment or delivery is postponed. For instance, purchasing a specific car in a showroom
transfers ownership at the moment of signing, even if the vehicle is collected later. However,
Section 21 provides that if the seller must do something to the goods to put them into a deliverable
state—such as polishing or packaging—ownership does not pass until that act is completed and
the buyer is notified. Similarly, under Section 22, if specific goods are deliverable but need
weighing or measuring to ascertain the price, title remains with the seller until those acts are done
and the buyer has notice, such as with scrap metal sold by weight.


In contrast, ownership of unascertained or future goods cannot pass until the goods are ascertained,
as mandated by Section 18. Under Section 23, for goods sold by description, property passes when
goods of that description, in a deliverable state, are unconditionally appropriated to the contract
with the assent of both parties. Assent may be express or implied and can occur before or after
appropriation. For example, when a seller separates and marks specific bags of cement for a buyer,
the act of appropriation transfers ownership. Conversely, ownership may pass when a buyer selects
specific timber planks from a merchant’s stock with the seller’s silent assent.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 31


 Finally, Section 24 governs goods delivered on a "sale or return" basis. Here, ownership passes to
 the buyer when they signify approval, adopt the transaction (such as by reselling the goods), or
 retain the goods beyond the agreed time for return without rejection. These statutory provisions
 collectively ensure certainty in commercial transactions by pinpointing the exact moment
 ownership is transferred.

         under Section 20.

         and neither party was at fault.

content.passageText:
Customary international law rests upon a dual-element foundation: State practice (the objective
 element) and opinio juris (the subjective element). State practice encompasses the tangible conduct
 of States, manifesting through diplomatic acts, legislative enactments, national court judgments,
 military manuals, and executive conduct. For such practice to generate customary law, it must
 meet qualitative requirements: it must be generally consistent (though not perfectly uniform),
 widespread and representative (including specially affected States), and may develop over either
 a lengthy or brief duration under the modern approach. A significant nuance concerns inaction,
 where silence or acquiescence may constitute practice, a principle illuminated by the Lotus case.


 The second element, opinio juris, distinguishes legal obligation from mere courtesy or political
 expediency. It requires that States believe the practice is legally compulsory. Evidence of this
 psychological element appears in government legal advisors' statements, treaty preambles, UN
 General Assembly resolutions, and diplomatic correspondence. The persistent objector doctrine
 provides a crucial paradox: a State that consistently objects during a custom's formation may
 exempt itself, thereby affirming the rule's binding force for others.


 Customary law assumes various forms and complexities. General custom binds all States
 universally, while special (regional/local) custom applies only to specific State groups, such as


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 34


 diplomatic asylum practice in Latin America. The relationship with treaties proves multifaceted:
 treaties may be declaratory of existing custom, serve to crystallize emerging custom, or generate
 rules that subsequently bind non-parties. The debate over "instant" custom questions whether
 norms can emerge rapidly from significant events without extensive practice.


 Participants in custom formation extend beyond States. International organizations contribute
 significantly, with UN General Assembly resolutions evidencing opinio juris. International courts,
 including the ICJ and ITLOS, influence development by identifying and articulating customary
 rules, while non-state actors increasingly shape normative expectations.


 At customary law's apex reside peremptory norms (jus cogens)—fundamental principles like
 genocide and torture prohibitions from which no derogation is permitted. These differ from
 ordinary custom through their non-derogable character. Relatedly, obligations erga omnes are
 owed to the international community as a whole. The orthodox inductive approach identifies
 custom by empirically examining practice and opinio juris, while the modern deductive critique
 observes that courts sometimes deduce rules from humanitarian logic rather than actual State
 practice, highlighting the persistent problem of proof in litigation.

Customary international law rests upon a dual-element foundation: State practice (the objective
 element) and opinio juris (the subjective element). State practice encompasses the tangible conduct
 of States, manifesting through diplomatic acts, legislative enactments, national court judgments,
 military manuals, and executive conduct. For such practice to generate customary law, it must
 meet qualitative requirements: it must be generally consistent (though not perfectly uniform),
 widespread and representative (including specially affected States), and may develop over either
 a lengthy or brief duration under the modern approach. A significant nuance concerns inaction,
 where silence or acquiescence may constitute practice, a principle illuminated by the Lotus case.


 The second element, opinio juris, distinguishes legal obligation from mere courtesy or political
 expediency. It requires that States believe the practice is legally compulsory. Evidence of this
 psychological element appears in government legal advisors' statements, treaty preambles, UN
 General Assembly resolutions, and diplomatic correspondence. The persistent objector doctrine
 provides a crucial paradox: a State that consistently objects during a custom's formation may
 exempt itself, thereby affirming the rule's binding force for others.


 Customary law assumes various forms and complexities. General custom binds all States
 universally, while special (regional/local) custom applies only to specific State groups, such as


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 34


 diplomatic asylum practice in Latin America. The relationship with treaties proves multifaceted:
 treaties may be declaratory of existing custom, serve to crystallize emerging custom, or generate
 rules that subsequently bind non-parties. The debate over "instant" custom questions whether
 norms can emerge rapidly from significant events without extensive practice.


 Participants in custom formation extend beyond States. International organizations contribute
 significantly, with UN General Assembly resolutions evidencing opinio juris. International courts,
 including the ICJ and ITLOS, influence development by identifying and articulating customary
 rules, while non-state actors increasingly shape normative expectations.


 At customary law's apex reside peremptory norms (jus cogens)—fundamental principles like
 genocide and torture prohibitions from which no derogation is permitted. These differ from
 ordinary custom through their non-derogable character. Relatedly, obligations erga omnes are
 owed to the international community as a whole. The orthodox inductive approach identifies
 custom by empirically examining practice and opinio juris, while the modern deductive critique
 observes that courts sometimes deduce rules from humanitarian logic rather than actual State
 practice, highlighting the persistent problem of proof in litigation.

content.passageText:
The Doctrine of Basic Structure represents one of the most significant judicial innovations in
 Indian constitutional law, emerging from the Supreme Court's effort to balance parliamentary
 sovereignty with constitutional supremacy. The constitutional crisis that necessitated this doctrine
 began with the conflict between Parliament's amendment power under Article 368 and the
 fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution. In the early years following
 independence, the Supreme Court had adopted a textual approach, holding in Shankari Prasad v.
 Union of India that Parliament possessed unfettered power to amend any constitutional provision,


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                              37


 including fundamental rights. This position was subsequently reaffirmed in Sajjan Singh v. State
 of Rajasthan. However, the political landscape shifted dramatically with the introduction of land
 reform legislations and the insertion of the Ninth Schedule by the First Amendment Act of 1951,
 which sought to place certain laws beyond judicial scrutiny.


 The conflict reached its zenith when Parliament enacted the Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth
 Amendment Acts in response to judicial decisions that threatened to limit its amendment power.
 It was against this backdrop that the thirteen-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
 delivered its landmark judgment in 1973, propounding the Basic Structure Doctrine. By a narrow
 majority, the Court held that while Parliament possesses wide powers to amend the Constitution,
 this power could not be exercised to destroy or damage the essential features or the basic structure
 of the Constitution. The precise contours of this doctrine were left undefined, with different judges
 offering varying formulations of what constituted the basic structure. Some identified fundamental
 rights, judicial review, secularism, and federalism as core components, while others emphasized
 the balance between different constitutional provisions. The doctrine operates as an implied
 limitation on the amending power, recognizing that an amendment power cannot include the power
 to completely abrogate the instrument from which it derives its authority.


 Subsequent years witnessed the doctrine being tested repeatedly, particularly during the
 Emergency period when the Supreme Court in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain applied it to
 strike down portions of the Thirty-ninth Amendment. The doctrine was further refined in Minerva
 Mills v. Union of India, where the Court held that the limited amending power itself constitutes a
 basic feature, ensuring that Parliament cannot convert its constituent power into an instrument of
 constitutional destruction.
