content.passageText:
Loneliness is no longer considered merely a personal misfortune; it is increasingly recognised as
 a public health emergency. Governments in the United Kingdom, Japan, and Australia have
 appointed ministers or commissioners specifically to address loneliness, a response historically
 reserved for infectious disease outbreaks. The impetus for this shift comes from a growing body
 of research. Chronic loneliness is associated with a 26% increased risk of premature mortality,
 effects comparable to smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. It raises the likelihood of heart disease,
 stroke, and dementia, while suppressing immune function and elevating levels of the stress
 hormone cortisol.Loneliness, however, is not synonymous with solitude. A person can live alone
 and feel deeply connected; another may be surrounded by people and feel profoundly isolated. The
 distinction matters because it points to the subjective nature of the condition: loneliness is a
 perceived gap between desired and actual social connection. This means structural interventions—
 building community centres, extending public transport to isolated rural areas, redesigning urban
 spaces to encourage incidental human contact—can reduce loneliness only if they also address the
 quality and meaning of social bonds, not merely their frequency.Critics of the public health
 framing argue that medicalising loneliness risks pathologising a normal human emotion and may
 divert resources from material poverty, housing insecurity, and employment precarity, which are


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                            44


 among its root causes. Others warn that state-led social connection programmes can feel coercive
 or hollow, especially for individuals whose isolation stems from grief, disability, or social anxiety.
 Support groups, befriending schemes, and community navigators have shown modest but
 consistent results in clinical trials, particularly when targeted at older adults and recent migrants.
 However, researchers caution that effect sizes are small, follow-up periods are short, and most
 studies lack adequate controls. Scaling what works in a pilot to an entire population remains an
 unsolved challenge. The broader consensus emerging from public health literature is that
 loneliness requires a multi-level response: one that combines individual support with the redesign
 of social infrastructure and a candid reckoning with the economic conditions that erode community
 life.[Extracted with revisions and edits from academic and public health sources on loneliness
 policy.]

I.     Fast fashion, the system of producing high volumes of cheaply made, rapidly changing
        clothing has transformed the global apparel industry over the past three decades. What was
        once a seasonal cycle of two collections per year has, for many retailers, become a near-
        continuous release of new styles, sometimes hundreds of micro-collections annually. The
        business model is designed around disposability: prices are low enough that garments are often
        worn only a few times before being discarded.The environmental consequences are severe.
        The fashion industry is estimated to account for around 10% of global carbon dioxide
        emissions, exceeding the combined output of the aviation and maritime shipping sectors.
        Synthetic fabrics such as polyester shed microplastic fibres during washing, which pass
        through wastewater treatment systems and accumulate in rivers, oceans, and ultimately in
        human tissue. Dyeing and finishing processes consume enormous quantities of water and
        release toxic chemicals; some of the most heavily contaminated rivers in the world flow
        through garment-producing regions of Bangladesh and Indonesia.Labour conditions represent
        a parallel concern. The 2013 collapse of the Rana Plaza complex in Dhaka, which killed over
        1,100 garment workers, illustrated the human cost of cost-cutting in global supply chains.
        Despite subsequent pledges by brands to improve factory safety and wages, investigations by
        labour rights groups consistently find that wage theft, excessive overtime, and unsafe working
        conditions remain widespread in supplier factories across South and Southeast Asia.
        Defenders of fast fashion argue that it has democratised clothing making style and self-
        expression accessible to people who could not previously afford fashionable dress and that it


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 47


       employs tens of millions of workers in economies with few alternative sources of formal
       employment. Some also contend that consumer choice and market pressure, rather than
       regulation, are the most effective levers for reform.However, critics respond that the
       affordability of fast fashion is possible only because environmental and social costs are
       externalised onto workers, communities, and future generations. Extended producer
       responsibility schemes, mandatory sustainability disclosures, and import duties linked to
       labour and environmental standards have been proposed as regulatory tools to shift these costs
       back to producers.[Extracted with revisions and edits from academic and policy sources on
       fashion industry sustainability.]

ENGLISH LANGUAGE
Sometimes, the most manifest gains are won after the most Herculean of battles. For France to
establish that “force is the crime” to establish that the use of force without consent causing
injury, rape, fear or annoyance is a criminal act, took years; extraordinary courage from one
woman, and an uprising where other women stood in solidarity with her. France has adopted a
law that defines rape as any non-consensual sexual act, a milestone for the women in the
country, but overall, a strike against sexual violence. The law was passed in response to urgent
calls from society to infuse consent into the law, and make sure that the law protects sexual
autonomy, particularly with reference to women. Last year, Gisèle Pelicot fought her toughest
battle when she took the stand in court, in a case accusing her husband of drugging and allowing
her to be raped by several men, some complete strangers. In December last year, the court
granted 51 convictions in the case, but it was more significant for establishing consent as a
pillar of law. It has been well established that survivors of sexual violence have an arduous
journey bringing their case to a court of law, and many women from disadvantaged social and
economic backgrounds, indeed do not have that privilege. There is a great deal of stigma, and
worse, judgement of the survivors in cases of rape, as recent public statements in India by
leaders blaming the women have painfully underlined again, and again. Even when a case of
rape enters the trial stage, the chances of securing a conviction are not encouraging. According
to the NCRB’s data, conviction rates for rape were between 27%-28% from 2018 to 2022. And
this, despite the fact that Section 129 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita recognises “criminal
force”.


To establish sexual autonomy as the cornerstone of the judicial process, while a first step, is
scarcely all. Preventing sexual violence will also involve shaping community views on gender
roles, dismantling rigid patriarchal codes with a measure of law, but also awareness
programmes that begin early, and orienting the police force to these principles, besides
funnelling resources into assisting survivors cope with the trauma. The road ahead is long and
arduous; for the journey of the survivors to be eased, governments should start with a complete
intolerance for sexual violence, and a commitment to stand by survivors, employing empathy
in the investigation and trial processes. To do any less, would be an injustice that would
interrupt the momentum of the women’s ‘Arab Spring’ Pelicot had set in motion.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/consent-is-all-on-sexual-violence-
support-for-survivors/article70226300.ece

The recent tragedy involving three minor sisters who stepped off a ninth-floor balcony together
in an act of collective despair has forced a harrowing reckoning with a new, endemic form of
addiction. These children had lived almost entirely within a gaming world for months –
reportedly insulated from reality and withdrawn from school. When their access was abruptly
severed to break the cycle, the resulting “void” proved too much to bear. For them, the scolding
was not merely a lecture; it was a perceived threat to the only domain in which he felt a sense
of achievement and agency. These cases underscore a terrifying reality: when the “digital
tether” is snapped by force, the resulting panic is not a tantrum – it is a clinical withdrawal.


With over 568 million active gamers, the world’s largest user base, India sees addiction rates
between 3.5 and 7.2 per cent among its youth. To address this, we must move past the label of
“bad behaviour” and understand the mechanics of capture. Expert analysis has highlighted how
children are caught in “Ludic Loops” – repetitive cycles of challenge and rewards meticulously


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                            6


designed by software engineers to be inescapable. When a child enters this state, they become
what experts call a “Digital Ghost.” They remain physically present at the dinner table but are
emotionally and psychologically absent. Their brain’s reward system has been rewired; the
nuanced pace of the physical world cannot compete with the high-speed chemical rush of the
screen. In this state, the child is responding to a deep chemical dependence where “unplugging”
feels like physical suffocation.


However, this biological capture does not occur in a vacuum; it is facilitated by a disappearing
physical reality. As we emerge as a global digital powerhouse, the question before us is whether
our physical “Third Spaces” for youth are vanishing under the weight of urban congestion and
high costs. Instead of reactive bans, we must advocate for “Safety by Design” rather than
punishment. The rising number of tragedies suggests that a shift in perspective is no longer
optional. We must realise the need for parental vigilance in the responsibility of building a
physical world worth inhabiting. This is a complex challenge involving biological,
psychological, and systemic factors. It is time to transform digital despair into real-world
connection by replacing force with empathy and systemic reform.

content.passageText:
Not too many years ago, you could watch endless YouTube videos with ease, but now you
must sit through unskippable ads to access the content you want—unless you pay. Twitter used
to be a space to collect news, engage with verified figures, and discuss world events, but is now
teeming with verified scammers. Instagram was once an app for posting and admiring cute
photos, but it now mimics TikTok and prioritises scrolling through algorithmically curated
viral and commercial short-form videos. Google helped you find articles of repute and
academic papers for projects, but now serves up an AI-generated mishmash of content that you
will have to further vet.


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                         8


What caused this degradation across your favourite platforms and apps? One theory that has
gained traction is enshittification: the feeling that many of your digital experiences,
transactions, and services are not improving over time but are actually becoming worse due to
their makers’ updates. Enshittification, according to Doctorow, is a way of naming the process
through which internet platforms are being made deliberately worse for customers, by their
decision-makers, until they decay completely. “Here is how platforms die: first, they are good
to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers;
finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then,
they die,” wrote Doctorow in a blog post in 2023. In other words: when your experience with
a shopping app or a streaming platform grows worse, much of this enshittification can be traced
back to the dominance of just a few Big Tech players, looser antitrust enforcement by
authorities, customers’ diminished capacity to control their digital experiences, and/or the
inability of tech workers to say no to exploitative bosses, according to the author.

Enshittification is also used to refer to a range of symptoms that degrade your experience as an
internet user or customer. Some examples include the insertion of advertisements, self-
preferencing by tech companies, unfair bias in search results, once-free features becoming paid,
genuine products being replaced with lower-value dupes, and more. Doctorow also points out
that apps offer massive potential for enshittification because app users often have less freedom
to block ads than users accessing the same platform via the web.

must sit through unskippable ads to access the content you want—unless you pay. Twitter used
to be a space to collect news, engage with verified figures, and discuss world events, but is now
teeming with verified scammers. Instagram was once an app for posting and admiring cute
photos, but it now mimics TikTok and prioritises scrolling through algorithmically curated
viral and commercial short-form videos. Google helped you find articles of repute and
academic papers for projects, but now serves up an AI-generated mishmash of content that you
will have to further vet.


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                         8


What caused this degradation across your favourite platforms and apps? One theory that has
gained traction is enshittification: the feeling that many of your digital experiences,
transactions, and services are not improving over time but are actually becoming worse due to
their makers’ updates. Enshittification, according to Doctorow, is a way of naming the process
through which internet platforms are being made deliberately worse for customers, by their
decision-makers, until they decay completely. “Here is how platforms die: first, they are good
to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers;
finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then,
they die,” wrote Doctorow in a blog post in 2023. In other words: when your experience with
a shopping app or a streaming platform grows worse, much of this enshittification can be traced
back to the dominance of just a few Big Tech players, looser antitrust enforcement by
authorities, customers’ diminished capacity to control their digital experiences, and/or the
inability of tech workers to say no to exploitative bosses, according to the author.

Enshittification is also used to refer to a range of symptoms that degrade your experience as an
internet user or customer. Some examples include the insertion of advertisements, self-
preferencing by tech companies, unfair bias in search results, once-free features becoming paid,
genuine products being replaced with lower-value dupes, and more. Doctorow also points out
that apps offer massive potential for enshittification because app users often have less freedom
to block ads than users accessing the same platform via the web.

SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/are-your-favourite-social-
platforms-being-degraded/article70228459.ece

content.passageText:
What’s in a military operation name? Quite a bit, actually. Despite being coordinated between
America’s Pentagon and Israel’s Kirya, Washington and Tel Aviv have decided to use two
separate op names for their Iran campaign – Op Epic Fury and Op Roaring Lion respectively.
Why two names? It’s all about political messaging. Having rechristened US’s department of
defence as department of war, Washington clearly wants to signal overwhelming power –
something that feeds into the narrative of US being No.1. Israel, meanwhile, is tapping into the
Judeo-Persian motif of the lion, signalling solidarity with old Persia against the Islamic
Republic.


All of these may seem like little mind games. But in the age of informationised warfare,
messaging is as important as cutting-edge drones. So, Op Midnight Hammer signalled a literal
battering of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure by US forces last year. But this exercise isn’t exactly
new. It all started with WWI and gained prominence in WWII, when Germany under Hitler
drew on historical and mythological figures to message German superiority. Hence, Op
Barbarossa – after Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I – for the German invasion of Soviet
Union.


US military began with colour-coded names such as Op Indigo – plan to prevent Nazis from
seizing Iceland – but later switched to a computerised naming system after Vietnam.
However, big ops get two-word names that are cleared by the Secretary of Defence, like Op
Enduring Freedom for Afghanistan and Op Odyssey Dawn for Libya. One exception: UK’s
op to retake the Falklands in 1982 was dubbed a very blah Op Corporate – said to be the next
available name on a Whitehall list. Closer home, we had India’s Op Cactus to thwart the
attempted coup in Maldives in 1988. If Op Parakram after the 2001 Parliament attack served
as a warning for Pakistan, Op Sindoor last year ensured justice for those widowed by the
Pahalgam terror attack. So, expect war names to get more creative, and political.


SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-edit-page/war-naming/

content.passageText:
CURRENT AFFAIRS

The recent electoral shift in Bharatiya Janata Party’s favour in West Bengal marks a significant
transformation in the state’s political landscape, traditionally dominated by regional forces like
the All India Trinamool Congress. Analysts attribute this outcome not merely to campaign
strategy but to a layered anti-incumbency sentiment that had been building over multiple
election cycles. Governance fatigue, allegations of corruption in welfare schemes, and internal
factionalism weakened the ruling establishment.

The BJP’s campaign leveraged central leadership visibility, grassroots mobilization, and a
narrative centered around governance efficiency and national integration. The party’s ability
to consolidate fragmented opposition votes, particularly in semi-urban belts, proved decisive.
Additionally, shifts in voter behaviour among youth and first-time voters reflected changing
aspirations tied to employment and development.


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                       13


However, the election also highlights broader themes in Indian democracy—how long-
standing regional parties face structural challenges when confronted with national parties
possessing stronger organizational machinery and financial resources. The role of federal
dynamics, electoral financing, and digital campaigning has become increasingly pronounced.

While the TMC’s decline appears sharp, political observers caution against premature
conclusions about its complete marginalization, noting that regional identity politics and
grassroots networks can facilitate resurgence. Nonetheless, the verdict signals a recalibration
of political equations in eastern India and underscores the evolving nature of electoral mandates
in the world’s largest democracy.

Source: The Hindu

CURRENT AFFAIRS

The recent electoral shift in Bharatiya Janata Party’s favour in West Bengal marks a significant
transformation in the state’s political landscape, traditionally dominated by regional forces like
the All India Trinamool Congress. Analysts attribute this outcome not merely to campaign
strategy but to a layered anti-incumbency sentiment that had been building over multiple
election cycles. Governance fatigue, allegations of corruption in welfare schemes, and internal
factionalism weakened the ruling establishment.

The BJP’s campaign leveraged central leadership visibility, grassroots mobilization, and a
narrative centered around governance efficiency and national integration. The party’s ability
to consolidate fragmented opposition votes, particularly in semi-urban belts, proved decisive.
Additionally, shifts in voter behaviour among youth and first-time voters reflected changing
aspirations tied to employment and development.


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                       13


However, the election also highlights broader themes in Indian democracy—how long-
standing regional parties face structural challenges when confronted with national parties
possessing stronger organizational machinery and financial resources. The role of federal
dynamics, electoral financing, and digital campaigning has become increasingly pronounced.

While the TMC’s decline appears sharp, political observers caution against premature
conclusions about its complete marginalization, noting that regional identity politics and
grassroots networks can facilitate resurgence. Nonetheless, the verdict signals a recalibration
of political equations in eastern India and underscores the evolving nature of electoral mandates
in the world’s largest democracy.

Source: The Hindu

content.passageText:
The fragile ceasefire between Iran and the United States has come under severe strain following
renewed hostilities in early May 2026. On May 4, Iran launched a series of missile and drone
strikes targeting infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates, including a major oil facility at
Fujairah. The attacks mark the first direct strike on a Gulf state since the ceasefire was declared
in April, raising concerns about a full-scale resumption of conflict.

The escalation is closely linked to tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global chokepoint
through which nearly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passes. Iran has effectively restricted
maritime movement in the region, while the United States has initiated military operations to
escort commercial vessels and restore navigation.

Global reactions have been swift, with multiple countries condemning the strikes and urging
de-escalation. The conflict has also triggered a sharp rise in global oil prices, reflecting fears
of supply disruptions and broader economic instability.

Analysts suggest that the renewed confrontation reflects deeper structural tensions, including
disputes over maritime security, regional influence, and stalled nuclear negotiations. While
diplomatic efforts continue, the situation underscores the volatility of the Gulf region and its
critical importance to global energy and geopolitical stability.

Source: The Guardian

technologies such as artificial intelligence.

LEGAL REASONING
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (TPA), serves as the foundational statute governing the
transfer of property between living persons in India, meticulously outlining the specific modes
through which such transfers can be lawfully effected. These modes, or specific transfers, each
possess distinct legal characteristics, rights, and obligations that are critical for the validity and
enforceability of the transaction. The first and most comprehensive mode is a Sale, defined
under Section 54 as the transfer of ownership in exchange for a price. It is a complete transfer
of all rights and interests from the seller to the buyer, fundamentally requiring a consideration
termed the price. A pivotal concept in a valid sale is that of a "marketable title," which refers


                                     12minutestoclat.com                                           21


to the seller’s ability to prove their ownership is free from reasonable doubt or litigation,
thereby ensuring the buyer receives a secure and undisputed interest in the property.


Another crucial mode is a Mortgage, involving the transfer of an interest in specific immovable
property for the purpose of securing a loan or the performance of an engagement. This area is
notably complex, encompassing various types such as a simple mortgage, where the property
is not delivered but the mortgagor binds themselves personally to repay; an English mortgage,
where the property is transferred absolutely to the creditor with a condition for re-transfer upon
repayment; and an equitable mortgage, created by depositing title deeds with the creditor. The
TPA meticulously delineates the rights and liabilities of both the mortgagor (the borrower) and
the mortgagee (the lender), including the mortgagor’s right of redemption and the mortgagee’s
power of sale. A Lease is a transfer of a right to enjoy a property for a specified period, in
consideration of a premium or rent paid periodically, and it creates a landlord-tenant
relationship distinct from full ownership. Conversely, a Gift involves the voluntary and
gratuitous transfer of existing movable or immovable property without any consideration, made
by a donor and accepted by the donee. The Act also recognizes an Exchange, where parties
transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, and the transfer of Actionable
Claims, which includes the transfer of rights to debts or beneficial interests in movable property
not in possession. Collectively, these defined modes provide a comprehensive legal framework
ensuring clarity, security, and fairness in all property transactions.

       his title is not marketable. Can she legally cancel the agreement?
options:
Yes, because a buyer has the absolute right to back out of any property deal before the
         final sale deed is registered, for any reason that they deem to be sufficient.

No, because the seller's provision of a legal opinion shifts the burden of proving title
         defects entirely onto the buyer, who must now complete the purchase.

Yes, because any doubt about the transaction, including price disputes, affects the
         marketability of the title and allows the buyer to withdraw from the agreement without
         any penalty whatsoever.


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        22

No, because the buyer cannot unilaterally cancel an agreement based on a price drop
        when the seller has already provided proof of a marketable title as required under the
        law.

content.passageText:
The architecture of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, rests upon a foundation of presumptions
and the principles of relevancy, meticulously detailed in its opening sections. Section 4 of the
Act introduces the crucial concept of presumptions, which are rules of law that dictate how a
court must or may approach certain facts. It delineates three distinct degrees. The first is when
the court "may presume" a fact, meaning the court enjoys a discretionary power to either regard
the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved, or to call for formal proof of it. The second


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        24


and stronger degree is when the court "shall presume". Here, the court is left with no discretion;
it is obliged to regard the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved. This creates a
mandatory presumption that shifts the evidentiary burden onto the opposing party. The third
and most absolute category is "conclusive proof". When a fact is declared to be conclusive
proof of another, the court is not permitted to entertain any evidence to the contrary. This
creates an irrebuttable presumption, where the existence of one fact is deemed to be the final
and incontrovertible truth of another.


Flowing from this framework of presumptions, the Act then establishes which facts are relevant
enough to be admitted for judicial scrutiny. Section 6 codifies the principle of res gestae,
rendering facts relevant that, though not strictly the fact in issue, are so connected with it as to
form part of the same transaction. This often applies to spontaneous declarations or
accompanying acts that lend veracity to the main event, such as the immediate outcry of a
victim. Expanding on this, Section 7 declares as relevant any facts which are the occasion,
cause, or effect of a fact in issue. For instance, the state of a lock after a burglary is relevant as
an effect of the crime. Furthermore, Section 8 establishes the enduring relevance of motive,
preparation, and conduct. While a strong motive may point towards guilt, and preparation
demonstrates a plan, the conduct of a person immediately after an alleged event—such as
fleeing the scene or attempting to dispose of evidence—is highly significant. Finally, Section
9 addresses facts which are necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue. This provision is
the legal basis for test identification parades, where the fact that a witness identified an accused
shortly after the crime helps to corroborate their testimony in court. Collectively, these sections
form the gateway through which facts must pass to be considered admissible, ensuring that
judicial proceedings are grounded in logically probative material.

options:
The court may presume the signature is genuine, but retains discretion to call for

The court must disregard the document entirely because the defendant has specifically
         denied his signature on it.


                                       12minutestoclat.com                                         25

The court must mandatorily presume the signature was genuine, and the defendant
       cannot challenge its authenticity.

No, because the presumption for ancient documents applies only to documents 30
       years old coming from proper custody.

content.passageText:
The architecture of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, rests upon a foundation of presumptions
and the principles of relevancy, meticulously detailed in its opening sections. Section 4 of the
Act introduces the crucial concept of presumptions, which are rules of law that dictate how a
court must or may approach certain facts. It delineates three distinct degrees. The first is when
the court "may presume" a fact, meaning the court enjoys a discretionary power to either regard
the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved, or to call for formal proof of it. The second


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        24


and stronger degree is when the court "shall presume". Here, the court is left with no discretion;
it is obliged to regard the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved. This creates a
mandatory presumption that shifts the evidentiary burden onto the opposing party. The third
and most absolute category is "conclusive proof". When a fact is declared to be conclusive
proof of another, the court is not permitted to entertain any evidence to the contrary. This
creates an irrebuttable presumption, where the existence of one fact is deemed to be the final
and incontrovertible truth of another.


Flowing from this framework of presumptions, the Act then establishes which facts are relevant
enough to be admitted for judicial scrutiny. Section 6 codifies the principle of res gestae,
rendering facts relevant that, though not strictly the fact in issue, are so connected with it as to
form part of the same transaction. This often applies to spontaneous declarations or
accompanying acts that lend veracity to the main event, such as the immediate outcry of a
victim. Expanding on this, Section 7 declares as relevant any facts which are the occasion,
cause, or effect of a fact in issue. For instance, the state of a lock after a burglary is relevant as
an effect of the crime. Furthermore, Section 8 establishes the enduring relevance of motive,
preparation, and conduct. While a strong motive may point towards guilt, and preparation
demonstrates a plan, the conduct of a person immediately after an alleged event—such as
fleeing the scene or attempting to dispose of evidence—is highly significant. Finally, Section
9 addresses facts which are necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue. This provision is
the legal basis for test identification parades, where the fact that a witness identified an accused
shortly after the crime helps to corroborate their testimony in court. Collectively, these sections
form the gateway through which facts must pass to be considered admissible, ensuring that
judicial proceedings are grounded in logically probative material.

       ambiguous to constitute relevant preparation.

Yes, because any act showing interest in poisons is always relevant in a poisoning
       case regardless of timing.

No, because preparation is only relevant if it involves actually acquiring the poison
       used in the crime.

Yes, because borrowing a book on poisons shows a plan to acquire knowledge about
       means to cause death.

content.passageText:
The Specific Relief Act, 1963, provides equitable remedies to enforce civil rights where
monetary compensation is inadequate. Part III of the Act deals with the Rectification of
Instruments, while Part IV governs the Rescission of Contracts. These provisions address two
distinct scenarios: correcting a written document to reflect the true agreement, or completely
canceling a contract when its formation was fundamentally flawed.


Section 26 of the Act empowers courts to rectify a written instrument that does not express the
real intention of the parties due to fraud or mutual mistake. The core principle is that a deed or
agreement should accurately mirror the actual contract between the parties. To obtain
rectification, the plaintiff must prove that a prior concluded contract existed and that, due to a
common error or fraudulent conduct, the formal document deviated from that agreement. The


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        27


court does not create a new contract but aligns the writing with the parties' genuine intent. Once
rectified, the instrument operates as if originally executed in its corrected form.


In contrast, Part IV (Sections 27 to 30) addresses the rescission of contracts, allowing a party
to have a voidable contract set aside. Rescission is typically available where consent was
obtained through coercion, undue influence, fraud, or misrepresentation. The party seeking
rescission must act promptly and generally restore any benefits received under the contract.
However, Section 27 provides specific defences against rescission. The court may refuse to
cancel a contract if the applicant has ratified it, expressly or impliedly; if, due to lapse of time
or third-party rights, the parties cannot be restored to their original positions; or if the contract
concerns a non-severable part of a property where the buyer has taken possession. These
defences ensure that rescission is not granted when it would be unjust or impractical.


Together, these provisions reflect the Act's commitment to substantive justice: rectification
polishes the instrument to reveal the true agreement, while rescission cancels the transaction
entirely when the foundation of consent is unsound, subject to protections for innocent parties
and practical limits on restitution.

content.passageText:
The constitutional scheme guaranteeing the right to freedom of religion, enshrined in Articles
25 to 28, establishes a delicate balance between individual liberty and collective religious
freedom. Article 25 provides for freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice,
and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part
III. This right extends to all persons equally, ensuring State neutrality in matters of faith. The
provision empowers the State to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other
secular activity associated with religious practice, thereby distinguishing between essential
religious practices and secular adjuncts.


Article 26 guarantees to every religious denomination the right to establish and maintain
institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage its own affairs in matters of religion,
own and acquire movable and immovable property, and administer such property in accordance
with law. This protection allows religious groups to operate autonomously, though the right to
administer property remains subject to State regulation to prevent mismanagement. Courts


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        30


have held that a denomination implies a collection of individuals united by shared faith,
possessing distinct legal identity for exercising these guarantees.


Articles 27 and 28 address specific dimensions of religious freedom. Article 27 prohibits
compelling any person to pay taxes for promotion or maintenance of any particular religion,
reinforcing secularism and preventing State endorsement of any faith. Article 28 prohibits
religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained by State funds, while
permitting such instruction in institutions established under endowments requiring religious
education, provided no person attending is compelled to participate without consent. For
minors, consent of guardians is required.


This framework accommodates individual autonomy and the character of religious institutions,
ensuring constitutional secularism remains resilient against majoritarian impulses or sectarian
conflicts. The equilibrium established by these provisions guides judicial interpretation when
conflicts arise between claims of faith and the constitutional order founded on justice, liberty,
equality, and fraternity. The protections underscore that religious freedom cannot be invoked
to justify practices undermining human dignity or the sovereign democratic character of the
nation.

The constitutional scheme guaranteeing the right to freedom of religion, enshrined in Articles
25 to 28, establishes a delicate balance between individual liberty and collective religious
freedom. Article 25 provides for freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice,
and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health, and other provisions of Part
III. This right extends to all persons equally, ensuring State neutrality in matters of faith. The
provision empowers the State to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other
secular activity associated with religious practice, thereby distinguishing between essential
religious practices and secular adjuncts.


Article 26 guarantees to every religious denomination the right to establish and maintain
institutions for religious and charitable purposes, manage its own affairs in matters of religion,
own and acquire movable and immovable property, and administer such property in accordance
with law. This protection allows religious groups to operate autonomously, though the right to
administer property remains subject to State regulation to prevent mismanagement. Courts


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                        30


have held that a denomination implies a collection of individuals united by shared faith,
possessing distinct legal identity for exercising these guarantees.


Articles 27 and 28 address specific dimensions of religious freedom. Article 27 prohibits
compelling any person to pay taxes for promotion or maintenance of any particular religion,
reinforcing secularism and preventing State endorsement of any faith. Article 28 prohibits
religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained by State funds, while
permitting such instruction in institutions established under endowments requiring religious
education, provided no person attending is compelled to participate without consent. For
minors, consent of guardians is required.


This framework accommodates individual autonomy and the character of religious institutions,
ensuring constitutional secularism remains resilient against majoritarian impulses or sectarian
conflicts. The equilibrium established by these provisions guides judicial interpretation when
conflicts arise between claims of faith and the constitutional order founded on justice, liberty,
equality, and fraternity. The protections underscore that religious freedom cannot be invoked
to justify practices undermining human dignity or the sovereign democratic character of the
nation.

content.passageText:
The early years of the Indian Republic were marked by significant challenges in implementing
socio-economic reforms, particularly in the agrarian sector. The government's ambitious
agenda of land reforms, aimed at abolishing the zamindari system and redistributing land to
the tiller, faced immediate legal hurdles. Zamindars and other landed interests, whose
properties were targeted for acquisition, began filing writ petitions in various High Courts,


                                   12minutestoclat.com                                       32


challenging the constitutional validity of these state-level land reform acts. They argued that
such laws violated their fundamental right to acquire and hold property, which was then
guaranteed under Article 31 of the Constitution. Fearing that a plethora of judicial rulings could
invalidate these crucial pieces of social welfare legislation and derail the entire reform process,
the central government resolved to take decisive constitutional action.


The response came in the form of the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951. This
amendment was a sweeping piece of legislation that introduced several significant changes to
the constitutional framework. Among its most innovative and enduring features was the
insertion of a new provision, Article 31B, and a corresponding new schedule to the
Constitution, the Ninth Schedule. Article 31B provided a unique and powerful legal umbrella.
It stipulated that any act or regulation placed in the Ninth Schedule would be deemed to be
valid and effective notwithstanding any judgment, decree, or order of any court or tribunal.
More critically, it stated that such laws could not be deemed void on the grounds that they took
away or abridged any of the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. The
Ninth Schedule itself was initially populated with thirteen specific acts, predominantly land
reform legislations enacted by various state governments.


The legal effect of this mechanism was profound. By placing a law within the protective ambit
of the Ninth Schedule, Parliament sought to grant it complete immunity from judicial review
on the ground of fundamental rights violations. This meant that a citizen could no longer
challenge the constitutionality of a Ninth Schedule law by arguing that it infringed upon their
right to equality, freedom of speech, or, most importantly, the right to property. The
constitutional validity of this novel arrangement was almost immediately challenged before the
Supreme Court.

Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971

content.passageText:
The doctrine of basic structure is one of the most significant innovations in Indian
constitutional law, serving as a judicial brake on the amending power of Parliament. It emerged
from the landmark Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala case in 1973, where the Supreme
Court held that while Parliament possesses vast powers to amend the Constitution under Article
368, it cannot destroy or damage its essential features or fundamental framework. This
principle was forged in response to conflicts between the judiciary and the executive branch,
particularly concerning land reform laws and the perceived assault on fundamental rights
during the 1960s and early 1970s. The Court reasoned that the term "amendment" inherently
implies change without altering the basic identity of the document, much like a person remains


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                      34


the same individual despite acquiring new clothes or undergoing physical changes. If
Parliament were allowed to rewrite the Constitution entirely or repeal its core elements, the
result would be a political transformation, not a mere amendment, and such power could not
have been intended by the framers.


The doctrine does not provide a fixed list of basic features, leaving the judiciary to determine
them on a case-by-case basis. However, over decades of adjudication, certain elements have
been consistently recognized. These include the supremacy of the Constitution, the rule of law,
the principle of separation of powers, the judicial review power itself, secularism, federalism,
the sovereign democratic republican character of the polity, and the mandate to build a welfare
state. In the Minerva Mills case, the Court further clarified that the power of judicial review is
so vital that its limitation or exclusion would violate the basic structure, and it also struck down
clauses that placed amendments beyond judicial scrutiny. The doctrine thus ensures that
transient political majorities cannot subvert the Constitution's foundational philosophy. It
establishes the judiciary as the ultimate guardian of the constitutional identity, empowered to
examine even constitutional amendments for their compatibility with the document's
overarching spirit. This uniquely Indian contribution to global constitutional thought has
allowed the Constitution to evolve responsively while maintaining its core integrity, balancing
flexibility with fundamental continuity.

content.passageText:
The pharmaceutical industry routinely defends its practice of making incremental
modifications to existing drugs, adjusting dosage forms, delivery mechanisms, or combining
active ingredients and then filing fresh patent applications on these reformulated products. This
strategy, known as "evergreening," effectively extends a drug's period of market exclusivity
well beyond the original twenty-year patent term. Defenders of the practice argue that it
rewards genuine innovation and incentivises companies to invest in improvements that benefit
patients.Critics, however, contend that evergreening is fundamentally a legal manoeuvre rather
than a scientific one. Most reformulations offer no meaningful therapeutic advantage over the
original compound. The new patent does not reflect a discovery that advances medicine; it
reflects a corporation's determination to delay the entry of cheaper generic competitors. In
markets where healthcare budgets are constrained, this delay carries a real cost: governments
and patients continue to pay premium prices for a drug whose core molecule has long since
ceased to be proprietary.India's response to this problem has drawn international attention.
Section 3(d) of India's Patents Act requires that, to be patentable, a new form of a known
substance must demonstrate significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy not merely a change
in form. Under this provision, the Supreme Court of India famously denied a patent extension
to a modified version of the cancer drug imatinib mesylate, ruling that the reformulation did
not cross the therapeutic efficacy threshold.The pharmaceutical industry challenged the Indian
provision vigorously, arguing that it sets an unusually high bar that will deter research
investment. But public health advocates responded that the standard is not punitive; it simply
ensures that patents reflect genuine medical advances rather than administrative creativity. The
core question in the evergreening debate is not whether pharmaceutical companies deserve to
profit from innovation; it is whether the law should reward paper innovation as though it were
the real thing.[Extracted with revisions and edits from discussions of pharmaceutical patent
policy and the Indian Patents Act.]

content.passageText:
Housing affordability has become one of the defining policy challenges of the twenty-first
century. In many cities, rising land values have pushed homeownership out of reach for
moderate-income households, even as governments struggle to fund conventional social
housing programmes. Community Land Trusts (CLTs) have emerged as one proposed solution
to this problem. Under the CLT model, a non-profit organisation retains permanent ownership
of land, while selling or leasing the buildings on it to individual residents at subsidised prices.
When a resident later decides to sell, the resale price is capped according to a formula that
allows only modest appreciation preserving affordability for the next buyer.Advocates argue


                                    12minutestoclat.com                                          43


that the model addresses the root cause of the affordability crisis. Because land, not the
structure itself accounts for the majority of urban property value, removing land from the
speculative market permanently breaks the cycle of escalating prices. CLTs that have operated
for decades in the United States and the United Kingdom report that homes remain affordable
across multiple generations of ownership, without requiring continuous government
subsidy.Critics, however, raise several objections. First, by capping resale gains, CLTs limit
the wealth-building opportunity that homeownership conventionally provides. A family that
purchases a CLT home cannot benefit from the full market appreciation that their neighbours
on freehold land enjoy. Second, scaling CLTs to a meaningful share of urban housing stock
requires substantial upfront public investment to acquire land, which many governments are
unwilling or unable to make. Third, some economists argue that restricting resale values simply
shifts the scarcity problem rather than solving it: the waiting list for affordable CLT homes can
be just as long as the waiting list for public housing.Supporters of CLTs respond that the
wealth-building critique misunderstands the model's purpose. CLTs are not designed to make
residents wealthy; they are designed to ensure that people with modest incomes have stable,
secure housing. Stability itself — freedom from eviction and from rent increases is a form of
economic security that conventional homeownership markets have failed to deliver to low-
income households.[Extracted with revisions and edits from academic and policy discussions
of Community Land Trusts.]

price. This strategy is designed to create a perception of a good deal while still maintaining a
reasonable margin.

10,000 but offers a complimentary perfume set worth Rs. 1,200 with every purchase. The cost
of this gift is borne by her and is treated as an additional expense while calculating her overall
profit.

Sometimes, the most manifest gains are won after the most Herculean of battles. For France to
establish that “force is the crime” to establish that the use of force without consent causing
injury, rape, fear or annoyance is a criminal act, took years; extraordinary courage from one
woman, and an uprising where other women stood in solidarity with her. France has adopted a
law that defines rape as any non-consensual sexual act, a milestone for the women in the
country, but overall, a strike against sexual violence. The law was passed in response to urgent
calls from society to infuse consent into the law, and make sure that the law protects sexual
autonomy, particularly with reference to women. Last year, Gisèle Pelicot fought her toughest
battle when she took the stand in court, in a case accusing her husband of drugging and allowing
her to be raped by several men, some complete strangers. In December last year, the court
granted 51 convictions in the case, but it was more significant for establishing consent as a
pillar of law. It has been well established that survivors of sexual violence have an arduous
journey bringing their case to a court of law, and many women from disadvantaged social and
economic backgrounds, indeed do not have that privilege. There is a great deal of stigma, and
worse, judgement of the survivors in cases of rape, as recent public statements in India by
leaders blaming the women have painfully underlined again, and again. Even when a case of
rape enters the trial stage, the chances of securing a conviction are not encouraging. According
to the NCRB’s data, conviction rates for rape were between 27%-28% from 2018 to 2022. And
this, despite the fact that Section 129 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita recognises “criminal
force”.


To establish sexual autonomy as the cornerstone of the judicial process, while a first step, is
scarcely all. Preventing sexual violence will also involve shaping community views on gender
roles, dismantling rigid patriarchal codes with a measure of law, but also awareness
programmes that begin early, and orienting the police force to these principles, besides
funnelling resources into assisting survivors cope with the trauma. The road ahead is long and
arduous; for the journey of the survivors to be eased, governments should start with a complete
intolerance for sexual violence, and a commitment to stand by survivors, employing empathy
in the investigation and trial processes. To do any less, would be an injustice that would
interrupt the momentum of the women’s ‘Arab Spring’ Pelicot had set in motion.

My two-year-old can spot Ambedkar anywhere. On the walls, in the streets, in photographs,
on the television. He’ll also point out if he sees someone wearing “Ambedkar kannadi”. The
same with Gandhi. He’s a Sanjay Subrahmanyan fan, and requests songs any time he meets
Sanjay maama. If only my husband and I could curate who gets to raise our son, we’d fill his
life with people and things that aligned with our beliefs like these. After all, we have curated
our own adult lives this way. Minimising interactions with those we are unable to reconcile
with on the important things. What I have discovered, however, is that it indeed does take a
village to raise a child.


Much as I want to be the primary influencer of his life, he is a being of his own, has always
been. And because he speaks, and he speaks a lot at so young an age, and because he isn’t
anxious about the world, and is looking at it with wonder and love, awe and joy, he has
interactions with several people, many ideas, vastly varied approaches to life every single day.
And it is impossible for me to handpick his world to be only touched by those whose
impeccable taste I approve of. It is his interactions with strangers that bring me the most delight
and, of course, concern.


And so, I’m trying to take the pressure off my son now, and apply it on to my own self — only
this time, to make myself softer. To set the example, by holding myself accountable to others,
I share my space with. By trying to figure out how to not fly into rage, and deal with conflict
with presence and control. To show him how much I love the softer things for him as well.
Embracing the Montessori way has helped somewhat at this stage, for it emphasises


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                              12 Minutes to CLAT


independence and shows us that the precious reward of learning is indeed self-sufficiency. I
am far from the perfect human, and one who’s painfully aware of her own shortcomings. And
I don’t expect to raise a mythical, perfect human son either. But if I were to apply one of the
many writing lessons to my life, in raising my son it is: Show, don’t tell.


After all, monkey see, monkey do.

The recent tragedy involving three minor sisters who stepped off a ninth-floor balcony together
in an act of collective despair has forced a harrowing reckoning with a new, endemic form of
addiction. These children had lived almost entirely within a gaming world for months –
reportedly insulated from reality and withdrawn from school. When their access was abruptly
severed to break the cycle, the resulting “void” proved too much to bear. For them, the scolding
was not merely a lecture; it was a perceived threat to the only domain in which he felt a sense
of achievement and agency. These cases underscore a terrifying reality: when the “digital
tether” is snapped by force, the resulting panic is not a tantrum – it is a clinical withdrawal.


With over 568 million active gamers, the world’s largest user base, India sees addiction rates
between 3.5 and 7.2 per cent among its youth. To address this, we must move past the label of

children are caught in “Ludic Loops” – repetitive cycles of challenge and rewards meticulously
designed by software engineers to be inescapable. When a child enters this state, they become
what experts call a “Digital Ghost.” They remain physically present at the dinner table but are
emotionally and psychologically absent. Their brain’s reward system has been rewired; the
nuanced pace of the physical world cannot compete with the high-speed chemical rush of the

content.passageText:
Not too many years ago, you could watch endless YouTube videos with ease, but now you
must sit through unskippable ads to access the content you want—unless you pay. Twitter used
to be a space to collect news, engage with verified figures, and discuss world events, but is now
teeming with verified scammers. Instagram was once an app for posting and admiring cute
photos, but it now mimics TikTok and prioritises scrolling through algorithmically curated
viral and commercial short-form videos. Google helped you find articles of repute and
academic papers for projects, but now serves up an AI-generated mishmash of content that you
will have to further vet.


What caused this degradation across your favourite platforms and apps? One theory that has
gained traction is enshittification: the feeling that many of your digital experiences,
transactions, and services are not improving over time but are actually becoming worse due to
their makers’ updates. Enshittification, according to Doctorow, is a way of naming the process
through which internet platforms are being made deliberately worse for customers, by their
decision-makers, until they decay completely. “Here is how platforms die: first, they are good
to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers;
finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then,
they die,” wrote Doctorow in a blog post in 2023. In other words: when your experience with
a shopping app or a streaming platform grows worse, much of this enshittification can be traced
back to the dominance of just a few Big Tech players, looser antitrust enforcement by
authorities, customers’ diminished capacity to control their digital experiences, and/or the
inability of tech workers to say no to exploitative bosses, according to the author.

Enshittification is also used to refer to a range of symptoms that degrade your experience as an
internet user or customer. Some examples include the insertion of advertisements, self-


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                            12 Minutes to CLAT


preferencing by tech companies, unfair bias in search results, once-free features becoming paid,
genuine products being replaced with lower-value dupes, and more. Doctorow also points out
that apps offer massive potential for enshittification because app users often have less freedom
to block ads than users accessing the same platform via the web.

SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/are-your-favourite-social-
platforms-being-degraded/article70228459.ece

content.passageText:
What’s in a military operation name? Quite a bit, actually. Despite being coordinated between
America’s Pentagon and Israel’s Kirya, Washington and Tel Aviv have decided to use two
separate op names for their Iran campaign – Op Epic Fury and Op Roaring Lion respectively.
Why two names? It’s all about political messaging. Having rechristened US’s department of
defence as department of war, Washington clearly wants to signal overwhelming power –
something that feeds into the narrative of US being No.1. Israel, meanwhile, is tapping into the
Judeo-Persian motif of the lion, signalling solidarity with old Persia against the Islamic
Republic.


All of these may seem like little mind games. But in the age of informationised warfare,
messaging is as important as cutting-edge drones. So, Op Midnight Hammer signalled a literal
battering of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure by US forces last year. But this exercise isn’t exactly
new. It all started with WWI and gained prominence in WWII, when Germany under Hitler
drew on historical and mythological figures to message German superiority. Hence, Op
Barbarossa – after Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I – for the German invasion of Soviet
Union.


US military began with colour-coded names such as Op Indigo – plan to prevent Nazis from
seizing Iceland – but later switched to a computerised naming system after Vietnam.
However, big ops get two-word names that are cleared by the Secretary of Defence, like Op
Enduring Freedom for Afghanistan and Op Odyssey Dawn for Libya. One exception: UK’s
op to retake the Falklands in 1982 was dubbed a very blah Op Corporate – said to be the next


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                            12 Minutes to CLAT


available name on a Whitehall list. Closer home, we had India’s Op Cactus to thwart the
attempted coup in Maldives in 1988. If Op Parakram after the 2001 Parliament attack served
as a warning for Pakistan, Op Sindoor last year ensured justice for those widowed by the
Pahalgam terror attack. So, expect war names to get more creative, and political.

content.passageText:
What’s in a military operation name? Quite a bit, actually. Despite being coordinated between
America’s Pentagon and Israel’s Kirya, Washington and Tel Aviv have decided to use two
separate op names for their Iran campaign – Op Epic Fury and Op Roaring Lion respectively.
Why two names? It’s all about political messaging. Having rechristened US’s department of
defence as department of war, Washington clearly wants to signal overwhelming power –
something that feeds into the narrative of US being No.1. Israel, meanwhile, is tapping into the
Judeo-Persian motif of the lion, signalling solidarity with old Persia against the Islamic
Republic.


All of these may seem like little mind games. But in the age of informationised warfare,
messaging is as important as cutting-edge drones. So, Op Midnight Hammer signalled a literal
battering of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure by US forces last year. But this exercise isn’t exactly
new. It all started with WWI and gained prominence in WWII, when Germany under Hitler
drew on historical and mythological figures to message German superiority. Hence, Op
Barbarossa – after Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I – for the German invasion of Soviet
Union.


US military began with colour-coded names such as Op Indigo – plan to prevent Nazis from
seizing Iceland – but later switched to a computerised naming system after Vietnam.
However, big ops get two-word names that are cleared by the Secretary of Defence, like Op
Enduring Freedom for Afghanistan and Op Odyssey Dawn for Libya. One exception: UK’s
op to retake the Falklands in 1982 was dubbed a very blah Op Corporate – said to be the next

Pahalgam terror attack. So, expect war names to get more creative, and political.

In 2026, India appointed a new Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), continuing the country’s push
towards military integration and defence modernisation. The office of the CDS was created to
improve coordination among the Army, Navy, and Air Force, particularly in areas such as
operational planning, procurement, and strategic policy.

significance following defence reform recommendations made after the Kargil conflict, which
highlighted the need for better inter-service coordination.

with distinct operational responsibilities. The Army is primarily responsible for land-based
military operations and remains one of the world’s largest standing armies. The armed forces
are overseen by civilian leadership under the constitutional framework of India.

The appointment comes amid growing emphasis on indigenous defence production, integrated
theatre commands, and modern warfare preparedness.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING
The legal framework governing obscenity in India underwent a paradigm shift in 2014 with the
Supreme Court's judgment in Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, which discarded the
archaic Hicklin test. For over 150 years, Indian courts had relied on the English standard from
Regina v. Hicklin, which judged a work by its potential to deprave vulnerable minds based on
isolated passages. The Aveek Sarkar case arose from a published photo story featuring tennis
star Boris Becker and his fiancée, alleged to be obscene. The Supreme Court explicitly rejected
the Hicklin test as outdated and out of step with constitutional morality.


In its place, the Court adopted the "contemporary community standards" test from American
jurisprudence. The new standard reorients the inquiry: the material must be considered as a
whole to determine if it predominantly appeals to a "prurient interest"—a shameful or morbid
interest in sex. Context is king; a work cannot be condemned based on a few passages.
Furthermore, the judgment provides a safe harbour by requiring courts to consider whether the
work possesses serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. This shift reflects a more
liberal, rational approach, recognising that not all depictions of sex are obscene.


Different media are governed by distinct frameworks. Print media operates without pre-
censorship but is subject to post-publication liability under the Indian Penal Code. In contrast,
films face a rigorous regime under the Cinematograph Act, 1952. The Act establishes the
Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), a statutory body tasked with pre-certifying films.
Section 5B mandates that the CBFC consider a film's impact on public order, decency, and
morality. Films are certified as 'U', 'UA', or 'A'. A key principle is the "adulteration" test, where
a scene so obscene that it "adulterates" the film's theme cannot be approved, often leading to
cuts. The constitutionality of this pre-censorship was upheld in K.A. Abbas v. Union of India


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                             12 Minutes to CLAT


 (1970), where the Supreme Court reasoned that films, due to their "mobility of image" and
 "realism," possess a greater capacity for evil impact and thus require prior restraint.

options:

A daily newspaper publishes an editorial cartoon that satirizes a current government policy.

   before publication to prevent potential indecency. The newspaper refuses. Can the

           whatsoever and cannot be regulated by any governmental authority.

LEGAL REASONING
The legal framework governing obscenity in India underwent a paradigm shift in 2014 with the
Supreme Court's judgment in Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, which discarded the
archaic Hicklin test. For over 150 years, Indian courts had relied on the English standard from
Regina v. Hicklin, which judged a work by its potential to deprave vulnerable minds based on
isolated passages. The Aveek Sarkar case arose from a published photo story featuring tennis
star Boris Becker and his fiancée, alleged to be obscene. The Supreme Court explicitly rejected
the Hicklin test as outdated and out of step with constitutional morality.


In its place, the Court adopted the "contemporary community standards" test from American
jurisprudence. The new standard reorients the inquiry: the material must be considered as a
whole to determine if it predominantly appeals to a "prurient interest"—a shameful or morbid
interest in sex. Context is king; a work cannot be condemned based on a few passages.
Furthermore, the judgment provides a safe harbour by requiring courts to consider whether the
work possesses serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. This shift reflects a more
liberal, rational approach, recognising that not all depictions of sex are obscene.


Different media are governed by distinct frameworks. Print media operates without pre-
censorship but is subject to post-publication liability under the Indian Penal Code. In contrast,
films face a rigorous regime under the Cinematograph Act, 1952. The Act establishes the
Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), a statutory body tasked with pre-certifying films.
Section 5B mandates that the CBFC consider a film's impact on public order, decency, and
morality. Films are certified as 'U', 'UA', or 'A'. A key principle is the "adulteration" test, where
a scene so obscene that it "adulterates" the film's theme cannot be approved, often leading to
cuts. The constitutionality of this pre-censorship was upheld in K.A. Abbas v. Union of India

Under Part II of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, Chapter II delineates the contours of specific
performance of contracts, with Sections 9 through 13 establishing a comprehensive framework
governing the enforceability of contractual obligations. Section 9 addresses the critical aspect
of defences available to a defendant in a suit for specific performance, establishing a statutory
presumption that a contract is capable of being specifically enforced until the contrary is
demonstrated. This provision effectively incorporates by reference the grounds enumerated in
Section 14, which specify circumstances where specific performance cannot be granted,
including situations where monetary compensation constitutes adequate relief or where the
contract is of such a trivial or minute character that its enforcement would serve no substantial
purpose.


The statutory scheme proceeds in Section 10 to delineate the affirmative cases where specific
performance becomes enforceable. This provision mandates the grant of specific relief when
the contracted act is of such nature that monetary compensation would prove inadequate, where
no standard exists for ascertaining actual damages, or where it appears probable that
compensation cannot actually be obtained. The section particularly emphasizes contracts
concerning immovable property, recognizing the unique character of land and the inherent
inadequacy of pecuniary remedies for its non-transfer.


Section 11 extends this remedial framework to contracts connected with trusts and fiduciary
relationships. Sub-section (1) enables beneficiaries to enforce contracts made for their benefit,
such as marriage settlements or trust deeds, despite not being original parties to the agreement.
Sub-section (2) addresses contracts by trustees or company directors holding property in
fiduciary capacity, permitting specific enforcement against them personally when they have
contracted to alienate such property.


The intricate provisions of Section 12 govern the enforcement of divisible contracts where
complete performance proves impossible. While sub-section (1) establishes the general rule
against partial enforcement, sub-sections (2) and (3) create exceptions where the unperformed
portion is relatively small and susceptible to monetary compensation. Sub-section (4) addresses
the particularly complex scenario of joint ownership, permitting a purchaser to compel


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                            12 Minutes to CLAT


 transferring co-owners to convey their shares while recovering compensation for the shares of
 non-consenting co-owners.


 Finally, Section 13 operates as a protective mechanism for purchasers and lessees contracting
 with persons lacking perfect title. This provision empowers the buyer to compel completion of
 the transaction should the vendor subsequently acquire good title, covering situations where
 the seller initially had no title, acted under mistaken belief regarding title, or had previously
 contracted to sell the property to another party.

content.passageText:
The procedural stages that form the skeleton of a criminal trial under the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, apply uniformly across all trials, whether before a Sessions
Court or a Magistrate. The first critical stage is the Framing of the Charge, which serves to
inform the accused of the precise accusation. In warrant trials, this involves a formal written
document detailing the specific offense. In summons trials for lesser offenses, the court merely
states the particulars of the offense in plain language. Closely related is the Joinder of Charges,
which allows trying a person for multiple offenses in a single trial to prevent multiplicity of
proceedings, provided the offenses are committed in the same transaction or within twelve
months.


However, not all cases proceed to a full trial. Withdrawal from Prosecution allows the Public
Prosecutor, with the court's consent, to withdraw from the case for valid reasons. Additionally,
Plea Bargaining offers a pre-trial negotiation where the accused voluntarily pleads guilty in
exchange for a lesser sentence, involving a formal application and, in compoundable offenses,
a settlement with the victim.


Once a trial commences, the core proceeding is the Examination of Witnesses. This follows a
structured pattern: Examination-in-Chief by the party calling the witness, Cross-Examination
by the opposite party to test veracity, and Re-Examination by the original party to clarify
matters arising from cross-examination. The entire process is governed by rules on the
Recording of Evidence, dictating how a judge must document depositions.


After the prosecution closes its case, the court mandates the Examination of the Accused under
Section 351 of the BNSS. This compulsory stage allows the accused to explain incriminating
circumstances appearing in the evidence, though they cannot be administered an oath.
Subsequently, the accused may lead Defence Evidence, producing witnesses and documents in
their support. Following the evidence, both sides present Arguments, final oral submissions
summarizing their case. The trial culminates in the Judgment, the final decision which must be
in plain language, contain points for determination, and be pronounced in open court. In
addition to sentencing, the court may issue an Order for Compensation, directing the accused
to pay monetary relief to the victim for the loss or injury caused.

In a case involving alleged murder, which is exclusively triable by a Sessions Court, the
   judge begins by reading out the allegations in simple language and asks the accused to plead
   guilty. The accused remains silent, and the public prosecutor objects to this procedure,
   insisting that a formal written charge must first be framed. Is the procedure adopted by the
   judge correct?
options:
No, because in warrant trials before a Sessions Court, the framing of a formal written
          charge detailing the specific offense is mandatory before the accused can be called
          upon to plead.

Yes, because the BNSS permits judges in all trials to dispense with formal charges
          and simply state the particulars of the offense in plain language to simplify
          proceedings for the accused.

Yes, but only if the accused is represented by counsel because if the accused is
          unrepresented then a formal charge must be framed to ensure proper understanding of
          the accusation.

No, because while summons trials require only particulars of the offense, sessions
          trials require a formal charge only when the accused pleads not guilty at the very outset
          of the trial.

          procedural rules.

content.passageText:
The Regulating Act of 1773 was the British Parliament's first direct intervention in the East
 India Company's Indian territories, seeking to address administrative mismanagement and
 establish central control. A cornerstone of this new structure was the reorganization of the
 Bengal government. The Act designated the Governor of Bengal as the Governor-General of
 Bengal, a position first held by Warren Hastings. To assist him and prevent absolute power,
 the Governor-General was to be aided by a council of four members, creating the Governor-
 General-in-Council. This answered the need for collective decision-making, yet the Act
 specified that all decisions were to be taken based on the majority vote of the council. This
 provision, intended as a check on the Governor-General's authority, frequently led to
 administrative deadlock.


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                            12 Minutes to CLAT


 Furthermore, the Act created a clear administrative hierarchy. The Governors of Bombay and
 Madras were explicitly brought under the superintendence and control of the Governor-General
 of Bengal and his Council in matters of war and peace, a crucial step toward centralizing
 authority. In the judicial sphere, the Act provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at
 Calcutta via charter in 1774. This court was vested with authority to try all cases, civil and
 criminal, against British subjects and their servants, creating a complex jurisdiction alongside
 existing Company courts.


 To address rampant corruption, the Act incorporated several provisions. It prohibited Company
 servants from private trade and from receiving gifts or bribes from natives. It also raised the
 salary of the Governor-General to discourage corruption and required the Court of Directors to
 report all correspondence regarding civil and military affairs to the British government.
 However, the Act did NOT establish a system of annual revenue collection assessments in
 Bengal; such mechanisms were developed later through separate regulations. The Regulating
 Act thus laid a foundational, albeit flawed, framework for the constitutional governance of
 British India.
