content.passageText:
The Constituent Assembly of India, a body conceived and elected for the singular purpose of
 framing a constitution for an independent nation, represents a pivotal chapter in Indian legal
 and political history. Its origins can be traced to the intellectual and political ferment of the
 early twentieth century, with the idea first being mooted by M. N. Roy in 1934. However, the
 demand for such an assembly was formally accepted by the British government for the first
 time through the Cripps Mission of 1942, which proposed a mechanism for Indians to draft
 their own constitution. This acceptance laid the groundwork for the eventual formation of the
 Assembly under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.


 The Constituent Assembly, constituted in 1946, held its inaugural session on 9 December 1946.
 It was during these early proceedings that the philosophical blueprint for the Indian Republic
 was laid down. Jawaharlal Nehru moved the historic Objectives Resolution on 13 December
 1946, a resolution that outlined the fundamental principles and the vision of the Constitution.
 This resolution, which later became the Preamble, was a momentous declaration of the
 Assembly's aims and ideals. After extensive debate and deliberation, the Objectives Resolution


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                               12 Minutes to CLAT


 was formally adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947, setting the moral and
 political compass for the work that lay ahead.


 The intricate task of giving legal shape to these objectives was entrusted to various committees.
 The most significant among them was the Drafting Committee, which was tasked with
 examining the vast array of materials, reports, and models to produce a coherent constitutional
 draft. This committee was composed of seven eminent jurists and scholars, whose expertise
 was instrumental in navigating the complexities of constitutional design. The committee
 worked tirelessly under the leadership of its chairman to prepare a draft that was then published,
 debated clause by clause, and subjected to intense scrutiny by the full Assembly.


 A unique aspect of the Assembly's composition was the representation of the Indian Princely
 States, which were not directly under British rule. These states were integrated into the
 constitutional framework through a process of negotiation and consultation. The
 representatives from these princely states were not elected by the public nor nominated by the
 British Crown. Instead, they were appointed by the heads or rulers of the respective princely
 states, ensuring that the diverse interests of these territories were voiced during the constitution-
 making process.

9 December 1946
22 January 1947

In the landmark case of State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale, the Supreme Court delivered
 a judgment that illuminated the transformative vision underlying Article 17 of the Indian
 Constitution. The case arose from incidents involving the enforcement of social disabilities
 against members of Scheduled Castes in a Karnataka village, where the accused were charged
 under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955. Beyond determining guilt or innocence, the
 Supreme Court used this opportunity to articulate the constitutional philosophy animating the
 abolition of untouchability.


 The Court observed that Article 17 and the Protection of Civil Rights Act represent far more
 than mere penal provisions. They embody what the Court described as "a vision of social
 revolution and the foundation of a new social order." This characterization reflects the
 understanding that the Constitution sought not merely to prohibit a practice but to
 fundamentally transform the hierarchical structure of Indian society. The provision was
 intended to dismantle centuries of entrenched social discrimination and to establish human
 equality as the bedrock of the new republic.


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                              12 Minutes to CLAT


 The Supreme Court emphasized that Article 17 operates as a constitutional mandate for social
 reconstruction. It rejects the notion that untouchability is a matter of private custom or religious
 practice beyond state interference. Instead, it affirms that the Constitution possesses the
 authority to declare certain social practices illegitimate regardless of their historical antiquity
 or religious sanction. The provision represents a conscious break with the past and a
 commitment to creating a society where human dignity is not determined by birth.


 The Court further observed that the Protection of Civil Rights Act must be interpreted in light
 of this constitutional vision. It is not a penal statute to be construed strictly in favor of the
 accused, but rather a remedial measure designed to give effect to fundamental constitutional
 values. The Act translates the constitutional prohibition into enforceable legal rights, creating
 mechanisms through which victims can seek redress and perpetrators can be held accountable.


 The judgment also addressed the sociological dimensions of untouchability, recognizing that
 the practice is sustained not merely by individual acts of discrimination but by deeply
 embedded social structures. The Court acknowledged that legal prohibition alone cannot
 eradicate centuries of prejudice, but affirmed that law has a crucial role in establishing new
 norms of social conduct. By declaring untouchability unlawful, the Constitution creates the
 normative foundation upon which social reform can proceed.
content.questionText:
Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability. Which of the following
   statements best describes the legal effect of this provision?
options: It merely directs the state to enact laws for the abolition of untouchability.

It renders the practice of untouchality legally void but requires legislation to prescribe
         punishment.

It operates prospectively, invalidating only those customs that arose after the
         Constitution's commencement.

 a judgment that illuminated the transformative vision underlying Article 17 of the Indian
 Constitution. The case arose from incidents involving the enforcement of social disabilities
 against members of Scheduled Castes in a Karnataka village, where the accused were charged
 under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955. Beyond determining guilt or innocence, the
 Supreme Court used this opportunity to articulate the constitutional philosophy animating the
 abolition of untouchability.


 The Court observed that Article 17 and the Protection of Civil Rights Act represent far more
 than mere penal provisions. They embody what the Court described as "a vision of social
 revolution and the foundation of a new social order." This characterization reflects the
 understanding that the Constitution sought not merely to prohibit a practice but to
 fundamentally transform the hierarchical structure of Indian society. The provision was
 intended to dismantle centuries of entrenched social discrimination and to establish human
 equality as the bedrock of the new republic.

 or religious sanction. The provision represents a conscious break with the past and a

content.passageText:
Urban parks are sometimes dismissed as luxuries — pleasant, but not essential. Yet the
 evidence tells a different story. Parks serve as natural sponges during heavy rainfall, absorbing
 water that would otherwise flood streets and homes. Trees within parks remove air pollutants
 and help cool cities by reducing the “heat island effect,” where concrete and asphalt trap
 warmth and raise temperatures. These environmental benefits directly reduce healthcare costs
 for city governments.

 Parks also shape the social fabric of a neighbourhood. Residents who live near well-maintained
 green spaces tend to interact more frequently with their neighbours, and research suggests that
 areas close to parks experience lower rates of crime. However, not every resident benefits
 equally. In many cities, wealthier, predominantly white neighbourhoods enjoy greater access
 to parks and better-quality green spaces than low-income communities and communities of
 colour. This gap matters because the health and social benefits of parks are directly linked to
 how close and accessible they are.

 Economically, parks are hardly passive assets. Businesses prefer to expand into areas with
 strong quality-of-life features, and parks are a key part of that picture. Property values in areas
 surrounding well-maintained parks rise noticeably. In one striking example from Atlanta,
 Georgia, a city plan to build an expensive underground stormwater reservoir was replaced by
 an above-ground green space with natural water features — saving the city over $16 million
 while also creating a public amenity. The lesson is clear: investing in parks is not a trade-off
 against practical urban infrastructure. It often replaces it entirely, delivering greater financial
 returns and social value to the city at a lower cost.

 [Extracted with revisions and edits from “Why City Parks Matter”, City Parks Alliance, and
 “Urban Parks Are Essential Infrastructure”, NMBL Strategies.]

content.passageText:
Urban parks are sometimes dismissed as luxuries — pleasant, but not essential. Yet the
 evidence tells a different story. Parks serve as natural sponges during heavy rainfall, absorbing
 water that would otherwise flood streets and homes. Trees within parks remove air pollutants
 and help cool cities by reducing the “heat island effect,” where concrete and asphalt trap
 warmth and raise temperatures. These environmental benefits directly reduce healthcare costs
 for city governments.

 Parks also shape the social fabric of a neighbourhood. Residents who live near well-maintained
 green spaces tend to interact more frequently with their neighbours, and research suggests that
 areas close to parks experience lower rates of crime. However, not every resident benefits
 equally. In many cities, wealthier, predominantly white neighbourhoods enjoy greater access
 to parks and better-quality green spaces than low-income communities and communities of
 colour. This gap matters because the health and social benefits of parks are directly linked to
 how close and accessible they are.

 Economically, parks are hardly passive assets. Businesses prefer to expand into areas with
 strong quality-of-life features, and parks are a key part of that picture. Property values in areas
 surrounding well-maintained parks rise noticeably. In one striking example from Atlanta,
 Georgia, a city plan to build an expensive underground stormwater reservoir was replaced by
 an above-ground green space with natural water features — saving the city over $16 million
 while also creating a public amenity. The lesson is clear: investing in parks is not a trade-off
 against practical urban infrastructure. It often replaces it entirely, delivering greater financial
 returns and social value to the city at a lower cost.

 “Urban Parks Are Essential Infrastructure”, NMBL Strategies.]

content.passageText:
Most people know that sleep is important, but many treat it as optional — something to sacrifice
 when work, study, or entertainment competes for time. This is a costly mistake. During sleep,
 the brain does not simply switch off. It actively consolidates memories, processing the
 information absorbed during the day and transferring it into long-term storage. Students who
 sleep well after studying retain more than those who stay up late reviewing the same material.

 Sleep also plays a powerful role in physical health. The body uses sleep to repair tissues,
 regulate hormones, and strengthen the immune system. During deep sleep, a specific type of
 immune cell becomes more active, which is why people who are sleep-deprived tend to fall ill
 more easily. Chronic poor sleep has been linked to a higher risk of conditions such as obesity,
 diabetes, and heart disease.

 A common objection is that some people simply function well on less sleep — that sleep needs
 are personal and vary widely. While it is true that individual needs differ slightly, researchers
 have found that most adults require seven to nine hours per night for optimal health. Those
 who believe they perform well on five or six hours are often measuring the wrong things: they
 may feel alert, but cognitive tests reveal measurable declines in their attention and decision-
 making. In short, the belief that one can train the body to need less sleep is not supported by
 the evidence.


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                             12 Minutes to CLAT


 Experts recommend consistent sleep schedules, avoiding screens in the hour before bed, and
 keeping the sleeping environment cool and dark. Screens are particularly problematic: the blue
 light they emit suppresses melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that it is time to
 sleep. Yet even a good sleep environment cannot compensate for a cultural attitude that treats
 sleeplessness as a virtue.

 [Extracted with revisions and edits from “Why Sleep Matters”, NIH News in Health, and
 “Sleep 101”, University of Michigan School of Public Health.]

ENGLISH LANGUAGE
Cricket ceased to be a gentleman’s game long ago. It’s played by men, but, it is as much a woman’s
sport today. India’s Class of 2025 announced that loud and clear Sunday midnight, as their
infectious joy on winning the World Cup was beamed into homes across the country. It has been
compared to the 1983 moment for men’s cricket in India, when Kapil’s Devils stormed Lord’s and
defeated an all-time great West Indian side. The euphoria of the ’83 win, in a country where the
only previous world champion was Ajit Pal Singh’s hockey team of 1975, kick-started cricket’s
transformation into a mass sport. The 1987 World Cup, played at home, telecast nationwide and
packaged as entertainment, was truly the moment cricket transcended its elite, metro origins and
began to find fans outside the big cities.


The IPL was the culmination of that journey, when cricket became an aspirational sport, a ticket
out of rural misery and urban poverty, for many starry-eyed young people. Harmanpreet Kaur’s
Class of 2025 illustrates this story even better. Kaur is from Moga, Punjab, and her deputy, Smriti
Mandhana, hails from Sangli, a small town in western Maharashtra’s sugar belt. There’s Kranti
Gaud from Ghuwara, Uma Chetry from Golaghat, Shree Charani from Kadapa, and Richa Ghosh
from Siliguri. Mumbai and Delhi, and state capitals such as Dehradun, Chandigarh, Shimla and
Hyderabad are represented, but the team is more a microcosm of India’s geographical spread and
economic diversity.


The players represent the hopes of single mothers and rural families that scraped out resources to
ensure that their wards got to live out their dreams. This transformation of cricket as a pan- Indian,
class-agnostic sport is an empowering story that calls for celebration. It has enormous social and
economic implications for a nation where many still see the girl child as a burden. The Class of
2025 are role models, and evidence of the potential of India’s girls and women.

It was late in the afternoon, and the light was waning. There was a difference in the look of the
tree shadows out in the yard. Somewhere in the distance cows were lowing and a little bell was
tinkling; now and then a farm-wagon tilted by, and the dust flew; some blue-shirted laborers with
shovels over their shoulders plodded past; little swarms of flies were dancing up and down before
the peoples' faces in the soft air. There seemed to be a gentle stir arising over everything for the
mere sake of subsidence -- a very premonition of rest and hush and night. This soft diurnal
commotion was over Louisa Ellis also. She had been peacefully sewing at her sitting-room
window all the afternoon. Now she quilted her needle carefully into her work, which she folded
precisely, and laid in a basket with her thimble and thread and scissors. Louisa tied a green apron
round her waist, and got out a flat straw hat with a green ribbon. Then she went into the garden
with a little blue crockery bowl, to pick some currants for her tea. Louisa was slow and still in her
movements; it took her a long time to prepare her tea; but when ready it was set forth with as much
grace as if she had been a veritable guest to her own self.


After tea she filled a plate with nicely baked thin corn-cakes, and carried them out into the back-
yard.


"Ceasar!" she called. "Ceasar! Ceasar!"


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                4


There was a little rush, and the clank of a chain, and a large yellow-and-white dog appeared at the
door of his tiny hut, which was half hidden among the tall grasses and flowers. Louisa patted him
and gave him the corn-cakes. In about half an hour Joe Dagget came. She heard his heavy step on
the walk, and rose and took off her pink-and-white apron. Under that was still another -- white
linen with a little cambric edging on the bottom; that was Louisa's company apron. She never wore
it without her calico sewing apron over it unless she had a guest. She had barely folded the pink
and white one with methodical haste and laid it in a table-drawer when the door opened and Joe
Dagget entered.


He seemed to fill up the whole room. A little yellow canary that had been asleep in his green cage
at the south window woke up and fluttered wildly, beating his little yellow wings against the wires.
He always did so when Joe Dagget came into the room.


"Good-evening," said Louisa. She extended her hand with a kind of solemn cordiality.

When Jammu and Kashmir lifted the Ranji Trophy this season, it was not merely a cricket result;
it was a quiet rewriting of a national narrative. For decades, the region’s name has surfaced in
headlines for reasons far removed from sport. Now it stands inscribed on the most coveted prize
in India’s domestic first-class game ~ and that shift carries weight far beyond the boundary ropes.
The Ranji Trophy is not the IPL’s glitzy cousin. It is the hard anvil on which India’s Test cricketers
are forged. To win it requires depth, temperament and the ability to grind through four-day contests
against teams steeped in tradition. This did not happen by accident. Institutional repair preceded
on-field triumph.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 6


The Jammu and Kashmir Cricket Association’s overhaul, the appointment of Mithun Manhas in
an administrative leadership role, and the professionalisation of coaching structures signalled that
sentiment alone would not suffice. Earlier interventions by Bishan Singh Bedi and Irfan Pathan
had chipped away at the psychological barrier that often dogs teams from the periphery ~ the quiet
doubt that they do not belong. That barrier has now collapsed. Leadership also mattered. Paras
Dogra, drafted in to anchor a rebuilding effort, brought the authority of experience. Around him
emerged a core that combined discipline with flair. Fast bowler Aquib Nabi’s 60-wicket season
was not a romantic flourish; it was the statistical backbone of a championship campaign.


For the young cricketers practising on winter mornings in Srinagar or Jammu, this title redraws
the map of possibility. It says that the route to the Indian team no longer runs exclusively through
Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru. It can begin in the valley, on grounds once overshadowed by curfews
and caution. Sport cannot resolve political complexities. But it can alter atmospheres. By winning
the Ranji Trophy, Jammu and Kashmir have claimed something simple yet profound: recognition
earned on merit. In doing so, they have moved from cricket’s margins to its centre, and forced the
rest of the country to adjust its gaze.

content.passageText:
When Jammu and Kashmir lifted the Ranji Trophy this season, it was not merely a cricket result;
it was a quiet rewriting of a national narrative. For decades, the region’s name has surfaced in
headlines for reasons far removed from sport. Now it stands inscribed on the most coveted prize
in India’s domestic first-class game ~ and that shift carries weight far beyond the boundary ropes.
The Ranji Trophy is not the IPL’s glitzy cousin. It is the hard anvil on which India’s Test cricketers
are forged. To win it requires depth, temperament and the ability to grind through four-day contests
against teams steeped in tradition. This did not happen by accident. Institutional repair preceded
on-field triumph.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 6


The Jammu and Kashmir Cricket Association’s overhaul, the appointment of Mithun Manhas in
an administrative leadership role, and the professionalisation of coaching structures signalled that
sentiment alone would not suffice. Earlier interventions by Bishan Singh Bedi and Irfan Pathan
had chipped away at the psychological barrier that often dogs teams from the periphery ~ the quiet
doubt that they do not belong. That barrier has now collapsed. Leadership also mattered. Paras
Dogra, drafted in to anchor a rebuilding effort, brought the authority of experience. Around him
emerged a core that combined discipline with flair. Fast bowler Aquib Nabi’s 60-wicket season
was not a romantic flourish; it was the statistical backbone of a championship campaign.


For the young cricketers practising on winter mornings in Srinagar or Jammu, this title redraws
the map of possibility. It says that the route to the Indian team no longer runs exclusively through
Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru. It can begin in the valley, on grounds once overshadowed by curfews
and caution. Sport cannot resolve political complexities. But it can alter atmospheres. By winning
the Ranji Trophy, Jammu and Kashmir have claimed something simple yet profound: recognition
earned on merit. In doing so, they have moved from cricket’s margins to its centre, and forced the
rest of the country to adjust its gaze.

content.passageText:
On February 7, 1976, the day Ritwik Ghatak died, Calcutta saw a spontaneous outpouring of grief.
Thousands of people thronged the streets and accompanied the funeral procession, paying homage
to the director who had died at 51 of tuberculosis. “It was a unique funeral of a unique man,” wrote
Safdar Hashmi in his 1981 essay, ‘The Genius That Was Ritwik Ghatak’. Yet, the profound public
mourning stood in sharp contrast to the neglect Ghatak endured in his lifetime. Despite being one
of the pioneers of India’s New Wave cinema, he had not received the kind of recognition his


12minutestoclat.com                                                                               8


contemporaries Satyajit Ray and Mrinal Sen enjoyed. His first film, Nagarik, would release only
after his death. Several others, including Titas Ekti Nadir Naam, would run into difficulties.


If Ghatak’s lifetime was marked by failure, the failure was heroic. He was perpetually at odds with
the system — political, cinematic, commercial — that demanded compliance. His films often
misunderstood, his politics unfashionable — he was expelled from the Communist Party in 1955
— his temperament uncompromising, he continued nonetheless to produce devastatingly beautiful
films, such as his Partition trilogy, Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960), Komal Gandhar (1961), and
Subarnarekha (1962), and nurtured a generation of filmmakers such as Mani Kaul, Kumar Shahani
and Adoor Gopalakrishnan during his stint as a teacher at Pune’s FTII. Ghatak saw cinema as a
social act that was both deeply local and radically universal, a form of collective memory-making,
as ritual and protest, as the world seemed to crumble all around him.


A century later, in a fractured world, his voice feels startlingly contemporary. It’s a reminder that
failure can be fertile, and that art, when it refuses to compromise, can be counted upon to bear
witness.

While there may be much relief after the détente in the tariff war between China and the U.S., in
Busan, South Korea, following the meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Chinese
counterpart Xi Jinping, the uneasy truce has laid bare a structural inversion of power between the


12minutestoclat.com                                                                             10


two economies. What began in the 1980s as a reluctant embrace of World Bank/IMF-prescribed
neoliberal reforms by an overwhelmingly agrarian China, has now evolved into an unimaginable
assertion of industrial dominance. A nation that once bartered sovereignty for technology transfer
and market access has, through patient accumulation of manufacturing depth, labour arbitrage, and
global supply-chain integration, positioned itself as the indispensable node of world production.
The irony is sharp. The U.S., whose export and technology corporations once defined global trade
cycles, now finds its four-year political rhythms ill-suited to contest a rival that plans in decades.
The concessions Mr. Trump has extended to Mr. Xi include some reductions in tariffs, a pause on
additions to the “no-trade list” of Chinese firms, and a partial rollback on levies linked to the
fentanyl supply-chain dispute. China has promised resumption of purchase of American farm
products, particularly soybean, and an easing of export restrictions on critical minerals.


America’s tariff offensives since Mr. Trump’s first term in 2017 did yield some numerical optics.
U.S. goods trade deficit with China narrowed by roughly 30%. But economists across the spectrum
agree that this was less a triumph of re-industrialisation than a diversion of trade flows. The deficit
was largely re-routed through near-shoring and friend-shoring: Mexico, Vietnam and parts of
ASEAN became new intermediaries for supply chains once centred in China. Meanwhile, China’s
exporters diversified markets and adjusted prices, while the tariffs’ direct burden was borne mostly
by U.S. importers and consumers. The human geography of the impact was asymmetric: in the
U.S., retaliatory Chinese tariffs targeted farm-belt commodities, hurting those very rural
constituencies that powered Mr. Trump’s rise. Federal subsidies softened the blow, but only
temporarily. In China, the pain was concentrated in export-processing hubs such as Guangdong
and Suzhou, where migrant and urban workers in electronics, semiconductor, and smartphone
assembly absorbed the shock. Yet, the political fallout remained contained, cushioned by Beijing’s
domestic-stimulus measures and its “dual-circulation” strategy of inward and outward rebalancing.
This trade war has thus underscored a decisive shift: the U.S. remains the world’s largest consumer
market, but China has entrenched itself as the world’s foremost factory with global leverage over
intermediate goods, high-end technology and critical minerals.

assertion of industrial dominance. A nation that once bartered sovereignty for technology transfer
and market access has, through patient accumulation of manufacturing depth, labour arbitrage, and
global supply-chain integration, positioned itself as the indispensable node of world production.

cycles, now finds its four-year political rhythms ill-suited to contest a rival that plans in decades.

products, particularly soybean, and an easing of export restrictions on critical minerals.

U.S. goods trade deficit with China narrowed by roughly 30%. But economists across the spectrum
agree that this was less a triumph of re-industrialisation than a diversion of trade flows. The deficit
was largely re-routed through near-shoring and friend-shoring: Mexico, Vietnam and parts of
ASEAN became new intermediaries for supply chains once centred in China. Meanwhile, China’s
exporters diversified markets and adjusted prices, while the tariffs’ direct burden was borne mostly
by U.S. importers and consumers. The human geography of the impact was asymmetric: in the
U.S., retaliatory Chinese tariffs targeted farm-belt commodities, hurting those very rural
constituencies that powered Mr. Trump’s rise. Federal subsidies softened the blow, but only
temporarily. In China, the pain was concentrated in export-processing hubs such as Guangdong
and Suzhou, where migrant and urban workers in electronics, semiconductor, and smartphone
assembly absorbed the shock. Yet, the political fallout remained contained, cushioned by Beijing’s
domestic-stimulus measures and its “dual-circulation” strategy of inward and outward rebalancing.

market, but China has entrenched itself as the world’s foremost factory with global leverage over
intermediate goods, high-end technology and critical minerals.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation, Shri Amit Shah today replied to the discussion
in the Lok Sabha on the no-confidence motion against the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Lok
Sabha rejected the no-confidence motion by voice vote, after discussion. Union Home Minister
and Minister of Cooperation said that this is not an ordinary event, and that a no-confidence motion
against the Speaker of the Lok Sabha has come after nearly four decades. He said that this is an
unfortunate incident for parliamentary politics and the House. Shri Shah said that the Speaker of
the Lok Sabha does not belong to any particular party but to the entire House, and is the protector
of the rights of all members of the House. He added that bringing a no-confidence motion against


12minutestoclat.com                                                                              16


the Speaker is not an act of courage. Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation, Shri Amit
Shah said that under Rule 374 of the Lok Sabha, in situations of disorder or indiscipline, the
Speaker has the authority to warn, name, expel, and suspend members. He said that those who
wish to agitate or act as activists within the House must conduct themselves according to the rules
of the House. Shri Shah said that under Rule 375, in the event of serious disorder, the proceedings
of the House have to be adjourned. He further said that under Rule 380, the Speaker has the
authority to expunge un-parliamentary words and remarks from the proceedings. He added that
un-parliamentary remarks made in a particular tone or context should not be preserved in the
history of Parliament, because doing so may lead future Members of Parliament to adopt the same
conduct. Shri Shah said that the list of un-parliamentary words has been developed over time by
many distinguished individuals who have held this office since the establishment of the House,
and it is binding on everyone.

content.passageText:
LEGAL REASONING
In March 2026, the Supreme Court of India in Union of India v. Rohith Nathan upheld the orders
of several High Courts that had directed the reconsideration of the ‘creamy layer’ status of Other
Backward Class (OBC) candidates appearing in Civil Services Examinations. The central
question before the Court was whether the income of parents employed in Public Sector
Undertakings (PSUs), private banks, or private organisations should be treated the same way as
the income of government employees when deciding whether a candidate falls within the creamy
layer.

The creamy layer concept was introduced through the Office Memorandum dated 08 September
1993, issued pursuant to the landmark judgment in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), which
upheld 27% reservation for OBCs in central government jobs but excluded the affluent among
them — labelled the ‘creamy layer’ — from availing the benefit. The idea was that reservation


12minutestoclat.com                                                                              24


should reach those who are truly socially and educationally backward, not those who are already
socioeconomically advanced.

The dispute in Rohith Nathan arose because the government had excluded income from certain
categories of employment when computing the creamy layer threshold for government servants,
but had not done so for candidates whose parents worked in PSUs, banks, or private firms. The
Court found that this differential treatment lacked a rational basis and directed the government to
reconsider the claims of such candidates under the 1993 Office Memorandum.

The ruling is significant because it reinforces the principle that the creamy layer test must be
applied uniformly and fairly. It also highlights the constitutional requirement under Article 16(4)
that the benefit of reservations must reach those who are genuinely backward, and that any
classification among OBCs for the purpose of creamy layer determination must be intelligible and
non-arbitrary. The judgment implicitly draws on the equality doctrine under Article 14, warning
that arbitrary distinctions within the same category of beneficiaries can render a policy
constitutionally vulnerable.

         despite having previously availed reservation at the state level.

Whether the 1992 Indra Sawhney judgment was validly decided and whether its creamy
         layer exclusion applied to all backward communities including SCs and STs.

Whether Article 16(4) empowers the government to set different percentage quotas for
         different sub-groups within the OBC category across all central examinations.

content.passageText:
A recurring question in motor accident compensation law is whether an insurance company can
escape its liability to pay compensation to accident victims merely because the driver of the
offending vehicle was found to be using a fake driving licence. The Supreme Court of India
addressed this issue decisively in Hind Samachar Ltd. v. National Insurance Co., reported in
(2026) 2 SCC, and laid down an important rule to protect accident victims.

The Court held that an insurance company cannot recover the compensation amount from the
vehicle owner simply because the driver was using a forged or fake licence. The insurer can only
seek such recovery — called a ‘pay and recover’ arrangement — if it is established that the vehicle
owner knowingly permitted a driver with a fake licence to operate the vehicle. In other words, the
mere fact that the licence turned out to be fake does not, by itself, absolve the insurer of its liability
to pay the claimant.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                    27


This ruling is anchored in the social purpose of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, which aims to ensure
that victims of road accidents receive prompt and adequate compensation without being made to
suffer for the internal relationship between the vehicle owner and the insurer. Section 147 of the
Act, which deals with mandatory insurance requirements, has been interpreted broadly by courts
to advance this protective intent.

The principle that emerges from this judgment is one of consumer protection applied in a tort law
context: the burden of proving that the owner knowingly allowed the breach falls on the insurer,
not the victim. This approach also discourages insurance companies from routinely raising
technical defences to delay or deny compensation to those injured in accidents, thereby reinforcing
the remedial character of the Motor Vehicles Act.

       arrangement after paying compensation in a motor accident case?
options:

         any identifiable mechanical defect or fault in the insured vehicle at the time.

Whenever the driver of the vehicle is found to have been using a fake or forged driving
         licence at the time the accident occurred on public roads.

Only when it is proven that the vehicle owner knowingly permitted a driver with a fake
         licence to operate the vehicle, placing the burden of proof on the insurer.

When the insurance policy had already lapsed before the date of the accident owing to
         non-payment of the applicable premium by the registered vehicle owner.

content.passageText:
In February 2026, the Supreme Court of India took a significant step in the field of prison reform
when it issued directions for the expansion and uniform governance of Open Correctional
Institutions (OCIs) across the country. The writ petition, filed under Article 32 of the
Constitution, raised concerns about severe overcrowding in prisons and the resulting violation of
the fundamental rights of prisoners, particularly the right to life and dignity guaranteed under
Article 21.

A Division Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta held that OCIs embody a
constitutional promise: that trust, responsibility, and graded liberty are essential for meaningful
rehabilitation of prisoners. Open prisons, unlike conventional closed prisons, allow convicts —
especially those who have served a substantial part of their sentence and have demonstrated good
conduct — to live in a relatively open environment, work, and maintain family ties.

The Court emphasised that overcrowding in regular prisons not only leads to inhuman conditions
but also defeats the reformative purpose of imprisonment. Addressing a prisoner as a human being
with rights — rather than simply as a person undergoing punishment — reflects the constitutional
philosophy underlying Articles 14, 19, and 21. The Court’s approach aligns with the Model Prison


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                30


Manual, 2016, which the Ministry of Home Affairs had recommended States adopt to modernise
prison administration.

The judgment reinforces the principle that imprisonment should serve both deterrent and
reformative purposes. Granting gradual freedom to eligible prisoners through OCIs, rather than
keeping all convicts in maximum-security settings until the last day of their sentence, is consistent
with this dual goal. The ruling also underscores the State’s positive obligation under the
Constitution to provide humane conditions in detention, making it a landmark in the evolving
jurisprudence of prisoners’ rights in India.

An injunction is a court order that either directs a party to do something (mandatory injunction)
or restrains a party from doing something (prohibitory injunction). It is an equitable remedy,
meaning it is granted at the discretion of the court and not as a matter of right. Under Indian law,
injunctions are primarily governed by the Specific Relief Act, 1963 and Order XXXIX, Rules 1
and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Injunctions can be temporary (interlocutory) or permanent. A temporary or interlocutory
injunction is granted during the pendency of a suit to preserve the status quo until the final decision.
A permanent injunction is granted by the court at the conclusion of the trial on the merits of the
case, and it permanently restrains or compels the party.

For a court to grant a temporary injunction, three essential conditions must be satisfied. First, the
applicant must establish a prima facie case — meaning there is a serious question to be tried, not
a definitive finding on the merits. Second, the balance of convenience must favour the applicant
— the court weighs the possible harm to the applicant if the injunction is refused against the
possible harm to the respondent if it is granted. Third, the applicant must show that refusal of the
injunction would cause irreparable injury — harm that cannot be adequately compensated by
money alone.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                  33


The Supreme Court of India, in the landmark case of Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh (1992),
clarified that these three conditions are conjunctive and not alternative. Each must be
independently satisfied. Courts are especially cautious in granting mandatory interlocutory
injunctions — those requiring a party to take positive action — since such orders significantly
disturb the status quo. In Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden (1990), the Supreme
Court held that a mandatory interlocutory injunction can be granted only where the applicant’s
right is clear and there is an urgent need to prevent grave injustice that cannot be undone later.

content.passageText:
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC)
with effect from 1 July 2024, retains and refines the category of inchoate offences — crimes that
are incomplete but nonetheless punishable. The term ‘inchoate’ derives from Latin, meaning
‘unfinished’. These offences recognise that the law must intervene at the planning stage itself to
prevent serious crimes from being carried out.

Chapter IV of the BNS groups three distinct inchoate offences together: abetment (Section 45),
criminal conspiracy (Section 61), and attempt (Section 62). Abetment occurs when a person
instigates, engages in a conspiracy, or intentionally aids another in committing an offence.
Importantly, the act abetted need not actually be committed — the abettor is still liable. Criminal
conspiracy under Section 61 is the agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal
act, or to accomplish a lawful goal through illegal means. The agreement itself is punishable,
provided there is a common object.

Under Section 61 of the BNS, if the conspiracy is to commit an offence punishable with death, life
imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment of two years or more, the conspirators are liable to the
same punishment as if they had abetted the offence. For lesser conspiracies, the punishment is
imprisonment up to six months, or a fine, or both. Crucially, for serious offences, no overt act
beyond the agreement is necessary to attract liability.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                              36


The Supreme Court in Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration) (1988) — a case arising out of
the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi — held that conspiracy is rarely proved by direct
evidence, and courts may infer it from the conduct and circumstances of the accused. The BNS
continues this approach, while also linking criminal conspiracy to modern threats such as
organised crime under Section 111. The rationale across all three inchoate offences is the same:
collective or preparatory wrongdoing poses a danger to society that justifies legal intervention
before the harm is realised.

content.passageText:
The Anti-Defection Law in India is contained in the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, which
was inserted by the ______________-. It was introduced to curb the menace of political
defections — a practice that had led to frequent floor-crossing and instability in governments
since the late 1960s. The phrase ‘Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram’ became a byword for this problem,
after a Haryana MLA switched parties multiple times in a single day in 1967.

Under the Tenth Schedule, a legislator (Member of Parliament or a State Legislature) is liable to
be disqualified if they voluntarily give up membership of their political party, or if they vote or
abstain from voting in the House contrary to any direction issued by their political party without
its prior permission. The Presiding Officer of the House — the Speaker in the case of the Lok
Sabha and State Assemblies, or the Chairman in the case of the Rajya Sabha — is the competent
authority to decide disqualification petitions.

The Supreme Court’s landmark judgment in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the
constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule. The Court struck down Paragraph 7, which had
sought to exclude the Speaker’s decisions from judicial review. The ruling established that while
the Speaker acts as a tribunal in deciding defection cases, their decisions are subject to judicial
review by the High Courts and the Supreme Court on grounds of mala fides, procedural lapses, or
constitutional violations.

In Padi Kaushik Reddy v. State of Telangana (2025), the Supreme Court criticised the Telangana
Assembly Speaker for prolonged delays in deciding disqualification petitions against MLAs who


12minutestoclat.com                                                                              39


had crossed over to another party. The Court directed the Speaker to conclude proceedings within
three months and called on Parliament to reconsider whether vesting this adjudicatory
responsibility in the Speaker — who is typically a member of the ruling party — continues to serve
the democratic purpose for which the Tenth Schedule was enacted.

LOGICAL REASONING


From a 14-month high of 6.2% in October, consumer price inflation moderated to 5.5% last month.
Much of this minor respite stems from a decline in the inflation rate of some food items. For
vegetables, it cooled from a 57-month peak of 42.2% to just under 30%, while foodgrain prices
rose at the slowest pace in 28 months, and pulses cooled to just over 5% after a prolonged spell of
double-digit spikes. Despite these pockets of relief, overall food inflation remained sharp at over
9% for the third straight month, with edible oil prices firming up 13.3%, the highest in 30 months
as a global price spike has coincided with an import duty hike by the Centre. It is no surprise that
coconut oil prices are up over 42%, even as items such as garlic (85.1%), potato (66.7%),
cauliflower, and cabbage (well over 40%) are pinching consumers. While recent conversations
about the economy have focused on decelerating urban demand, the price rise trend is hitting rural
consumers harder with close to 6% inflation in November and higher food prices. Despite
assertions by the government that food prices are volatile and should be ignored for monetary
policy purposes when growth is stumbling, higher spending on meals is spilling into other items’


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                42


prices. Manufacturing and services firms have reported intensifying cost pressures last month,
compelling them to hike prices at the highest pace in 12 years.


The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which had originally estimated October-December inflation to
average 4.8%, raised it to 5.7% at its monetary policy review last week. This implies inflation this
month — which will be the last data before the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets
next — could still be high at 5.4%. This would be well above the central bank’s median target of
4% — the MPC now expects average inflation to attain that level only by the second quarter of
2025-26. The government, whose clamour for an interest rate cut was ignored by the MPC last
week, may be hoping its new appointee at the helm of Mint Street, another Finance Ministry
insider, may oblige with more urgent and bigger rate cuts to support growth. While some assert a
rate cut in February’s MPC meet is virtually cemented, going by current trends, the data may not
back such a move as growth might recover a bit and inflation may cool a tad more, thus diminishing
any urgency. That the Centre would have presented its Budget 2025-26 by the next MPC meet,
may help the rate cut case going forward, if it demonstrates fiscal prudence and steps to ease
citizens’ living costs.
SOURCE: https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/price-worries-on-
inflation/article68978440.ece

On November 27, a 60-day ceasefire deal between Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Israel, brokered by
the United States (US) and supported by France, came into effect. Since late September, exchanges
of fire between Hezbollah and Israel had escalated significantly. Over the subsequent months,
Israel employed extensive airstrikes targeting high-ranking leaders, including Hezbollah chief
Hassan Nasrallah, along with the group’s arsenal, launch sites, and critical crossings at the
Lebanese-Syrian border, aiming to degrade Hezbollah’s capabilities.


Iran’s missile barrage into Israel on October 1, ostensibly a response to the killing of Nasrallah
and Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, failed to deter Israel’s intensifying operations in Lebanon and
instead provoked direct Israeli retaliation against Iran. Iran’s restrained response, including support
for ceasefires in Gaza and Lebanon, reflects a strategic calculus shaped by regional geopolitics and
its defensive priorities.
Since the 2006 Hezbollah-Israel war, Iran has fortified Hezbollah with an extensive arsenal of
drones and rockets, intending these forward-strike capabilities as a deterrent against Israel. Over
the past year, Iran and Hezbollah pursued a strategy of escalation management, absorbing losses
to avoid outright war with Israel. Iran’s “axis of resistance,” comprising groups like Hezbollah and


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                  47


Hamas, has historically served as a deterrent framework, not as a mechanism for provoking full-
scale conflict involving Iran.
Iran’s strategy has emphasized a “unified fronts” approach—encouraging Hezbollah to open a
northern front and Houthis to disrupt Red Sea shipping and southern Israeli ports—to pressure
Israel into a Gaza ceasefire. However, Israel’s superior intelligence, air power, and US support
facilitated a separation of the Lebanon and Gaza fronts. The resultant weakening of Hezbollah
leaves Iran exposed to Israeli action and diminishes the axis’s deterrent credibility, evident in
emboldened Turkish-backed jihadist offensives in Syria.


Regional dynamics further explain Iran’s apparent restraint. Since October 2022, Iran has
intensified diplomatic efforts to rally support for a Gaza ceasefire and maintain rapprochement
with Riyadh and other Arab capitals. Iran’s regional diplomacy aims to counter US-backed
normalization between Israel and Gulf states while avoiding actions that might align Gulf
neighbors more closely with Israel. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi’s regional
engagements have emphasized Tehran’s interest in conflict de-escalation and securing assurances
against regional facilitation of Israeli or US aggression.
Parallel to its regional strategy, Iran has renewed overtures to the West on the nuclear issue and
proposed a new regional framework to reduce reliance on US influence. By encouraging Gulf
states to prioritize regional stability and avoid past insecurity linked to Trump’s “maximum
pressure” campaign, Iran seeks to forestall further escalation and preserve its strategic interests.
SOURCE:             https://www.hindustantimes.com/opinion/behind-iran-s-restraint-in-west-asia-
conflict-101734109533831.html

content.passageText:
The problem with marriage, we all know, is the endlessness of it. Plenty of things we do will have
long-term repercussions, but in what other situation do you promise to do something for the rest
of your life? Not when you choose a college. Not when you take a job. Not when you buy a house.
During childhood, you pick up many habits that are probably going to be lifelong, like walking,
talking, reading, and sleeping, but once you’ve got those down, you start to feel like you’re at
greater liberty to decide what things you want to do and what things you want to stop doing.
Especially when you’re a young adult the apparently infinite multiplicity of possible choices—
possible jobs, possible friends, possible cities, possible girlfriends or boyfriends—can sometimes
fool you into thinking you have an infinite amount of time to try out everything. But once you’re
married, you’ve significantly cut down the options, and it suddenly makes your life feel shorter—
like now there’s a direct line between you and your own death. You’ve just gotten on a train and
you won’t get off until the very end of the track. In your final moments, if you stick to your
promise, you’ll still be doing the same thing you’re doing now, dealing with the same person,
possibly having the same arguments. And that commonality between now and then makes that far-
off time, when you’re old and sick and about to die, a little more imaginable. Which is scary.
Apparently even my father didn’t quite escape this predicament. Although they were no longer
married, my mother was still there with him in the hospital on the day he died of lung cancer at
age sixty. And she even managed to subject him to one of their old familiar rituals, though he
wasn’t exactly in a condition to notice. Apparently after the nurse declared him dead and
shepherded me, my sister and my two aunts out into another room, while we were all hugging and
crying, my mother stayed in the room with my father’s body in order to give him a final piece of
her mind. “How could you?” she asked him. “How could you take such bad care of yourself and
abandon your two kids like this?” My parents had been divorced for over fifteen years, and my
father was dead, but my mother wanted to get in one last good fight.
SOURCE: https://thepointmag.com/examined-life/a-matter-of-life-and-death/

The 1945 atomic bombs that killed more than 200,000 people in Japan would today be called
“tactical” nuclear weapons. The survivors of those “tactical” nuclear weapons are the real experts
on what nuclear war means. They crawled through the rubble of the world’s first, and thankfully
only, nuclear war. It is cynical indeed for armchair warriors, particularly those with ties to the
companies building nuclear weapons, to advocate strategies based on unproven theories, not real-
life experience.


It is estimated that 38,000 children were killed in the attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The fact
that so many children were killed, maimed and harmed in other lingering ways in the attacks
motivated the survivors, like Taniguchi, who served as chair of the Nagasaki Council of A-Bomb
Sufferers for many years, to devote their lives to working to ensure no one ever again has to suffer
as they did.


The testimony of the survivors graphically shows that the idea that nuclear war can be fought and
won on the battlefield is dangerous, grotesque nonsense that makes nuclear war more likely. As
Annie Jocobsen’s recent book Nuclear War: A Scenario made clear, the use of a nuclear weapon
would quickly escalate and result in a major exchange that would not just kill tens or hundreds of
thousands near the explosions but would end the world as we know it in a matter of minutes. It
would cause a nuclear winter that would lead to the collapse of food production, famine and the
deaths of billions of people. The impact on global biodiversity and the economy is nearly
impossible to imagine.


The leaders of all the nuclear-armed countries need to ignore the siren voices that tell them nuclear
war can be fought and won and instead listen to the hibakusha who are urging them to eliminate
their arsenals before it is too late. The United Nations Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear
Weapons bans nuclear weapons and all activities associated with them outright. It came into force
in 2021 and half of all countries have already signed or ratified it. The TPNW provides the pathway
under international law for all nuclear-armed states to get rid of their weapons. This year’s Nobel


12minutestoclat.com                                                                               52


Peace Prize underlines that the governments of these countries have no more excuses – they should
join the treaty and eliminate their arsenals.
SOURCE:        https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2024/12/12/its-time-the-world-understands-a-
nuclear-war-cannot-be-won
